speechtext: Mr. ROBERT BICKERDIKE (Montreal, St. Lawrence) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 133) to prohibit the Importation, manufacture or sale of cigarettes.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Explain.

The Bill provides practically what is contained in the resolution that the House, by a very large majority, recently adopted. The Bill is founded on that resolution. It goes so far as to prevent the importation, manufacture and sale of cigarettes. I understand that this Bill may not be strictly regular, but I would ask, if necessary, that the House would suspend the rule, so that we may get the first reading. If there is any further explanation that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) requires I would be very glad to give it to him.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I do not take exception to the Bill being presented, nor do I raise any point as to the rule, but if I understand the resolution that was passed in this House a short time ago, it demands that the government, and not a private member, should introduce this legislation. This Bill, as I understand it, somewhat affects the revenue, and it is only the government that can deal with it. In view of that, the government should accept the responsibility for this Bill and see that it is passed into law. Either the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bickerdike) should hand it over to the government and let them carry out the mandate of the House of Commons contained in that resolution, or else the government should now declare that they will take the responsibility for it.

My hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) is somewhat in error when he wants to minimize the powers of the members of this House. A member of this House cannot in-

traduce a measure which would put any burdens upon the people, but a member of this House can always introduce a measure which will decrease the taxation and take burdens off the people, and, as I understand it, in this case the objection of my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) does not apply. I would also remind my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) that the government was not unanimous when the vote was taken on that resolution. It was looked upon as a question upon which the government were not called upon to formulate any policy.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I understand that the government are simply the servants of this House, and when the majority of this House commands the government^ to intopduieje legislation the government should not attempt to shirk the responsibility which is cast upon it by a large majority of the members of this House.

speechtext:
House resumed adjourned debate on the proposed motion of the Minister of Finance :
That Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee to consider of the Ways and Means for raising the Supply to be granted to His Majesty ; and the proposed motion of Mr. Borden (Halifax) in amendment thereto.
Mr. EDWARD HACKETT (West Prince, P.E.I.) Mr. Speaker, in rising to make a few observations on the important matters now under discussion, I may have to traverse a good deal of ground which has already been gone over ; but I feel it a duty incumbent upon me, representing an important constituency in Canada, as well as in justice to myself, to make some remarks on this all-important question. We are discussing, Sir, the fiscal policy of our country, the expenditure of the country, the taxes of the people ; and, therefore, I feel that it is the duty of every representative of the people to state his views in parliament, and state them with candour and frankness, in order that the public interests may, if possible, be advanced. What we want in Canada is a well-defined policy, not a shifting or mixed-up policy. We have been listening during the last few days to speeches by lion, gentlemen who have commenced those speeches, by announcing themselves as free traders or tariff-for-revenue men, but have ended by proclaiming themselves to be great protectionists. There is no sincerity in that. What we want is a well-defined policy, such as that propounded in the amendment proposed by the hon. leader of the opposition, a policy of protection in aid of industries, in fact, a policy of Canada for the Canadians.
What have we heard from hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House ? We had the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Roche) the other evening, in a very long speech, stating that he was pleased with the tariff of this government, that he was a tariff-for-revenue man, while towards the end of his speeeh he asked for more protection for iron and coal, which are very important industries in the province of Nova Scotia. Then, we had yesterday a very long speech from the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes), who also declared himself to be a supporter of a tariff-for-revenue, or if possible a free trade tariff ; but he wound up by saying : There is an industry in the riding I represent which should be protected -the salt manufacturing industry. Note the inconsistency and contradiction of his first statement. He said that to protect the salt industry in West Huron the government should tax the fishermen's salt, which now comes into this country free. Sir, I represent a district in which there reside a large number of fishermen, toilers of the sea, who follow the most precarious industry in Canada, going out on the water in their vessels and small boats to procure a living for themselves and their families. When the national policy 64

was introduced in 1879, I had the honour of being a member of this House, and it was regarded as a policy of compensation, so that if the fishermen of the maritime provinces had to pay a duty on flour coming from the province of Ontario, the residents of Ontario had to pay a duty on coal from the maritime provinces ; but the only protection given to the fishermen was in having free salt. Free salt is a most important commodity to the fishermen, and it has been free ever since the introduction of the national policy in 1879 until to-day, when the hon. member for West Huron, a supporter of the present government, comes out and advocates its taxation. I want, for a moment or two, to say a word in connection with the speech made by the hon. member for Haldimand. That hon. gentleman, I must say, spoke fluently and ably, but there was one element absent from his remarks, and that was the element of sincerity, and the absence of that quality completely destroyed his argument. In referring to the administration and policy of the Conservative party from 1878 down to 1896, and speaking more particularly on the subject of exhibitions, he said :
I will admit that there is some excuse for hon. gentlemen opposite in having taken no part in exhibitions in various parts of the world during 1895, for so far as I know in those dark days of Conservative rule, there was nothing in Canada of sufficient magnitude and nothing wonderful enough in workmanship to deserve an exhibition, unless it was deficits, and so far as I know, no prize was offered for these in any of the exhibitions of the world.
Well, Mr. Speaker, we had deficits but we had surpluses as well, to which I will refer later. But what I want at present to call the hon. gentleman's attention to is the Columbian exhibition, held in Chicago in 1893, at the time when this country was enjoying the benefits of Conservative rule. What do we find, Sir ? We find that at that exhibition the greatest in the past century-the greatest on this continent at least during this past century-Canada made a splendid showing and carried off large prizes, both in cash and other awards of merit. In the fine arts, horticulture, agriculture, live stock, dairying-in fact in all the departments at that exposition, Canada bore away numerous prizes, and yet we have this hon. gentleman say that there was no exhibition made by Canada in those days except one of deficits. Let me refer more specially to a letter which we find in the report of our commissioner, Mr. Lark, and which was written to him by a gentleman from Austria :
Brunn, Austria, December 20, 1893.
I have examined very carefully all the exhibits of Canadian textiles, and I am full of admiration of nearly all those beautiful exhibits which show the enormous progress the Canadian industry has made. The textiles exhibited were highly creditable as well in the department of cottons and woollens as in silks. Canada has, in my opinion, made most wonder-

ful progress in the sixteen years which have elapsed since the Centennial Exposition, and I can candidly say no other nation which exhibited, has shown such progress as Canada.
Here we have this letter from an exporter of textile fabrics residing in Austria, stating that no nation in the world had made such progress in manufacturing as Canada had during the sixteen years between the holding of the Centennial and the Columbian expositions-could any one require a more convincing contradiction of the statement of my lion, friend from Haldimand ? For my part, it seems to me that when an lion, member rises to address this House, when he speaks for his constituents to an intelligent, deliberative body such as this, he should state the facts.
Another matter to which the hon. gentleman referred was our public expenditure, and in thisi connection he put down to the credit of the government the amount of increased subsidy paid the province of Prince Edward Island. That expenditure, he said, pointing to myself, is one to which that hon. gentleman would at least not object. Sir, two years ago in this House, when that increased subsidy was proposed, I approved of it, but at the same time I said to the government:	You are only giving a sop to
the province of Prince Edward Island; yon are not giving that province a tithe of what is due it and what was solemnly guaranteed it on its entrance into confederation. This money was not given the province which I represent as an increase in its subsidy, but as some slight compensation for the loss sustained by it through its lack of communication with the mainland during the winter season.	.
In another matter to which he referred was the relieving of our canal system of tolls. The government, he said, were making our canals as free as the ocean. Well, Mr. Speaker, that may be all right to western and central Canada, but what is the government doing for the people of Prince Edward Island ? Making the canals free ns the ocean will not advance one iota the carrying out of the terms of confederation entered into between the Dominion a id Prince Edward Island in 1873. The hon. gentleman boasts of the surplus of $13,000,000 which) we are going to have this year. Well, we have the estimate of the most celebrated engineer in the world, Sir Douglass Fox, that $12,000,000 would be sufficient to construct a tunnel between the province of Prince Edward Island and the mainland, and if this government desires to And a place in which to appropriate its surplus to advantage, it will at once enter into a contract to have that tunnel constructed between the island, and the mainland. In this way it will not only carry out its contract with the province and relieve the people of that province from the disadvantages under which they are suffering, but will benefit the people of Canada from Vancouver to Halifax.

The hon. Finance Minister, in hisi budget speech spoke of the prosperous times we were enjoying in Canada at present, aud gave all the credit to this government, but it seems toi me that while he was making that statement the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce made a rather wry face. During the administration of Canadian affairs, while that hon. gentleman was Finance Minister, we had not the prosperous and growing times which we have to-day. On the contrary, from 1873 to 1878, was the era of the greatest depression that ever prevailed in Canada. We have the Finance Minister (Hon. Mr. Fielding) taking credit to the government for our present prosperity, but we had in those days the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) trying to escape responsibility for the bad times then existing by saying : We are only flies on the wheel and can do nothing to assist the country. But the Right Hon. Sir John Macdonald brought forward the policy of Canada for the Canadians and protection to Canadian industry. We will no longer, he said, submit to our country being made a slaughter market for the merchants and traders of the United States, but will adopt a tariff that will protect our own manufacturers. That policy was approved by the people and was followed by the most beneficial results. If we have prosperous times to-day, are we to attribute them to this government ? Not at all, Sir. I challenge hon. gentlemen opposite to show one act of legislation or administration introduced by them that has in any way been the1 cause of prosperity. If we are enjoying prosperity, it is not due to any legislation of this government, but to the fact that times are good the world over. Those hon. gentlemen opposite have not done anything, they have not initiated a single measure that in any way has contributed to tlie welfare or prosperity of our people. On tile contrary, I believe that if a Conservative government were in power at Ottawa, a government that could take advantage of tlie situation, a government that would have made the most of the prosperity which was just beginning to dawn the world over, when these hon. gentlemen opposite took office, Canada to-day, instead of only being fairly prosperous, would be a beacon of prosperity for all the nations of the world. In this connection, let me call your attention for a few moments to a comparison between the United States and Canada in order to show you that during the eighteen years that the national policy was in force in its entirety, before it had been emasculated and partly destroyed by hon. gentlemen opposite, the increase of exports from Canada was in greater ratio than the increase of exports from the United States. Hon. gentlemen opposite have not ventured to go the full length of their pledges. They have retained a part of that protective policy, and had they not done so they would have been long since forced from power. But, hav-

ing retained part of the national policy, though they destroyed it in part, Canada has gone on and prospered fairly well. Reference has been made to exports. 1 have here the figures showing the increase of exports of Canada in comparison with the increase of exports of the United States from 1878, to 1896 and from 1896 to 1902 :

About the same time that the present tariff was introduced in Canada the Congress of the United States made large additions to the protective duties under the Dingley law, and the result was that the United States exports increased even more rapidly than our own. Hon. gentlemen opposite say that Canada is prosperous, that she has gone on by leaps and bounds. It is true, but our prosperity has gone on only in concert with that of the rest of the world. What has caused that prosperity ? It was caused by the policy of the late administration by the statesmanship of the Right Hon. Sir John A. Macdonald and his associates. I remember the occasion in this House, in 1S79, when Sir Leonard Tilley brought down the national policy. That policy was opposed by every hon. gentleman on the treasury benches who was then in the House. But that policy was put in force, and became the policy of the country. And it has remained the policy of the country ever since, though as I say, it has been emasculated and its usefulness to a certain extent taken away by hon. gentlemen opposite. But if those hon. gentlemen would go to the country with the fads they had at one time- 64}
free trade as they have in England, Commercial Union, unrestricted reciprocity-instead of wearing the leavings of the clothes of the Conservative party, they would not have the slightest chance of returning to power.
Hon. gentlemen opposite boast that the immigration into Canada has increased. We know that there is large immigration into the North-west, and we are proud of it. We have in that country the most fertile wheat fields in the world, tens of millions of acres awaiting to be occupied. When, in 1880, Sir Charles Tupper brought down to parliament the project to build the Canadian Pacific railway how was that project met by these hon. gentlemen opposite 1 They opposed it, as they opposed the national policy, by every means fair and foul, even to the extent of getting up bogus syndicates to take the place of the syndicate that had been given the charter to build the work. Yet, in the face of all their opposition, the contract was let and the work completed. And, if we are enjoying prosperity in Canada to-day if there is a large immigration going into the North-west, it is largely due to the ability of the statesmen who were then in control of the destinies of Canada. I had the honour of being a member of this House when both these great measures, the national policy and the Canadian Pacific railway contract were introduced. I well remember the stand, the unmanly, dishonest stand, taken by hon. gentlemen on the other side, then in opposition. Now, they boast of the prosperity of the country, but that prosperity is due, as I have said, to the statesmanship of the Liberal-Conservative party, under the leadership of the Right Hon. Sir John A. Macdonald, with Sir Charles Tupper and Sir Leonard Tilley as his lieutenants.
We have had some changes in the tariff. Hon. gentlemen opposite, when they assumed power, declared themselves opposed to specific duties and in favour of ad valorem duties. They made the change, and what has been the result ? Values have increased and the taxpayers of Canada are paying more to-day for goods purchased under this ad valorem system than ever before. We have the taxes of the people increased from $28,000,000 to $38,000,000, as was shown by the hon. member for South Leeds (Mr. Taylor) who addressed the House last evening, these taxes being levied on the necessaries of life in many instances. Hon. gentlemen opposite introduced the preferential tariff, and their policy was lauded to the sky. It was said to be a great thing for Canada and for the empire for it would draw closer the bonds which bind the parts of the empire together. But what did the right hon. Mr. Chamberlain say at the conference of colonial premiers 1 He declared that the preferential tariff was of no service to Great Britain. And I have no doubt that It Is disappointing to the gentlemen who In-

troduced It. It lias proved a failure, and the Finance Minister stated the other day that it was only a matter of time when they would probably repeal the preferential tariff.
Now, Sir, I must return for a moment to the bon. member for Haldimand. He referred to an increase of $100,000 in the fishery service of this country, and be said it was mainly due to the erection of cold storage buildings and for the benefit of fishermen in the maritime provinces. Now, I have in my hand a statement which shows that so far as Prince Edward Island is concerned that money was not expended in any such manner; no part of that increase was due to any assistance rendered to the fishermen, but it was due to the extravagance, and perhaps worse, of the fishery officers in that province. But the strange part of this showing is, what becomes of the money ? How do they expend it ? I remember when the inspector of fisheries, in 1900, came up to West Prince on what he called a sporting trip, shooting partridges if you will, iu the month of October, but actually for the purpose of canvassing votes against the gentleman who now represents West Prince in this parliament. It was apparently proper for him to travel at the expense of the people of this country, and to run up this tremendous bill which I have read to you for his travelling expenses and outlay, so long as he was doing the work of the machine that is operated by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House.
It is not my intention, Mr. Speaker, to occupy much longer the time of the House.

The hon. gentleman from Huntingdon (Hr. Muclaren) made a calculation yesterday that it costs the country $28 a minute to run this parliament. As I wish to save the people's money, I think it would be only right to make my speech as brief as possible. We hear a great deal about the wonderful resources of this Canada of ours, with its wealth of forest, as yet untouched by the axe of the woodman, with mines of gold, silver and coal, with fertile lands unequalled in any part of the world, with fisheries of unexcelled and vast wealth, with an enterprising population, energetic, industrious and virtuous. Why should we not go on and prosper ? Why should hon. gentlemen opposite endeavour to tie the hands of this young giant that is now beginning to put forth his strength ? All that is required to guarantee our progress is to give proper encouragement to the people of Canada. Do not let us drive them off to the United States to look for employment in a foreign land. In the province from which I come, there was a falling off in our population from the census of 1891 to that of 1901, of over 5,000. Whether the latter census was taken correctly or not, X will not say at present. But these young men and young women have gone away because they could not find employment in Canada, because avenues of industry were not afforded them at home ; and they went to seek their fortune in a foreign land and beneath a foreign sky. Sir, the great national policy inaugurated by the Liberal-Conservative party in 1879 is the policy that must stand for the people of this country. The amendment moved by the leader of the opposition is in the right direction. It is an amendment to afford adequate protection, which means sufficient protection-hon. gentlemen opposite understand the meaning of the word quite well enough-it means sufficient and proper protection for the interests of the people of Canada, for the labourer, for the manufacturer, for the fisherman, for the miner, for all the industries of Canada. That is what we need for Canada, and hold* ing those views, I shall have much pleasure in voting for the amendment moved by my hon. friend for Halifax (Mr. Borden.)

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the progress of this debate some very important statements have been made which have brought out some situations worthy of notice. The hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) in delivering his budget, stated clearly, I think, the reasons why he has decided that there should be no changes in the tariff at the present time. He did not say that there should be no changes for one year, or two years, or for a number of years, but he said at the present time. He gave as a reason for this de-cison the buoyant condition of the general business of the country. Last year the cry of the opposition in the matter of the tariff centred almost entirely upon the one item
of woollens. Not one specific statement has been made, not one special complaint has been delivered by the opposition, but they have confined themselves to general questions and they Ifave not indicated so far any particular line of trade or commerce that is suffering at the present time. The surtax proposed to be imposed on German goods will probably meet to a large extent, if not entirely, their objections, so far as the woollen trade is concerned. Now, we do not hear any specific complaints so far as any other line of manufacture is concerned. It is no more than fair in criticising the budget speech that statements should be specifically made. Yet, the opposition have so far not even contended that there are any special lines of trade requiring changes in the tariff in order to ensure their success and prosperity. If we take note of the reports of the annual meetings of the cotton companies which have been lately held we will find that they state business to be good. They have declared fair dividends. Some of the companies have declared dividends even so high as 9 per cent. That would indicate that there is really no cause for serious complaint as regards cottons. Any man who has been in business for the last few years knows thoroughly well that in almost every line of business the only difficulty has been that the manufacturers have not been able to supply goods in sufficient quantity to meet the demands of the people of the country. Scarcely any line of business furnishes quotations which are not subject to withdrawal at any moment and a large number of manufacturers, especially in the iron lines sent out quotations which are not standard quotations. This has been the case for several years. It is not a question of holding Canada for the Canadians, but it has been absolutely impossible for the Canadian manufacturers for the last few years to fill the orders offered to them, and the result is that the people of Canada have been obliged to go abroad to buy a lot of the goods which they require and which have been brought into this country. That statement is borne out by the fact that there is scarcely a manufacturing concern in the Dominion of Canada but is adding to its plant to enable it to get out the orders offered to it. Manufacturing plants are being increased all over the Dominion. The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) stated again his position in regard to adequate protection, but he did not deign to go into details or to make any specific statement as to what he meant by adequate protection. So far as he is concerned this House has been left entirely in the dark and we have had to get our information otherwise, and that information lias been forthcoming from several quarters. When the hon. member for St. Mary's, Montreal (Hon. Mr. Tarte) made a statement of his position, and he said that lie be-| lieved he was speaking to a large extent

for the people of Canada, he said that the duties should be raised to an average of 50 per cent upon dutiable goods coming into the country. When he made that statement it was loudly applauded oh the opposition side of the House by hon. members generally and by the leaders particularly. That indicated that the hon. gentlemen had expressed their position upon that matter. They agree with the hon. member for St. Mary's, Montreal, that the tariff should be upon the basis of an average duty of 50 per cent and the hon. member for South Leeds (Mr. Taylor) has gone so far as to say: Yes, and even 100 per cent, if necessary. Upon this point the position of the two parties to-day are well defined. The position is definitely stated upon the Liberal side of the House in the speech of the hon. Minister of Finance. He has indicated that the tariff as it stands to-day shall be the tariff for the future. He has indicated that the tariff stands to-day and as it has stood for the last four or five years, shall not be interfered with, at all events at present. On the opposition side of the House the position has been taken, not definitely by the leader, but practically definitely by the party, that the average rate of duty must be from 50 per cent up to 100 per cent. I am pleased personally that the issue has become so plainly defined. So far as X am concerned, and so far as the county which I represent is concerned, I am pleased the definition is so plainly before us. I am satisfied with the plain definition before us.
I should be pleased to have the hon. member for South Leeds travel over the county of Glengarry and address meetings after the style he was indulging in last evening, and I think, so far as Liberalism in Glengarry is concerned, he would fix it sure and fast for many generations to come. The opposition wish to raise the tariff wall so high that all the goods required in this country shall be manufactured in this country. Now, if all the goods required in this country were manufactured in this country where would we get the revenue ? From what source will the country draw its money to carry on the public affairs ? Will the public debt be reduced or be paid off if such a policy as that is in force ? If we were to manufacture all the goods in this country we could have no revenue and if taxation is to be at the rate of 50 per cent to 100 per cent then we have the right to ask where shall we get the money to carry on the business of the country. If we look back to the Conservative regime of eighteen years previous to the advent of this administration we find that to a certain extent they did carry out this policy. We find that they were not able to scrape revenue enough together to carry on the business of the country then without increasing the public debt. We are all well aware that the debt was increased during that time by over $150,000,-
000.	That is the policy they proposed to Mr. SCHELL.
put in force if they should come back to power to-morrow. And what is to be done with the money obtained from this increase of duties amounting from 50 to 100 per cent ? The hon. member for St Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) told us that the manufacturers of Canada numbered two or three hundred individuals.

speechtext: I did not say two hundred; I said several hundred.

speechtext:
Well, we will say that they number a few hundred. But I would remind the House that not all the manufacturers of Canada have asked for increased duties. I doubt if half of them have asked that the duties should be increased. Suppose there are two hundred manufacturers all told, and that half of them want the duties increased, then if their request is acceeded to, this half of the manufacturers of Canada will have the privilege of taxing the farmers and the workingmen from 50 to 100 per cent more than at present, and where will that money go. Will it go to pay the debt of this country or to develop our resources ? Not one cent of it. These manufacturers are not asking that that increased taxation shall go into the business of the country, or go to pay the running expenses of the government, but they ask that it shall go into their own pockets, and that the success of their business and their profits shall be guaranteed by Act of parliament. That is what they want. I well remember the change of government in the year 1896, and I remember how the Conservatives claimed that it was a mistake of Providence to put the Liberals in power. After the elections of 1896 the leaders of the Conservative party and many of their supporters still retained their seats here, and they proclaimed in this House that the instinct of government was with the Conservatives, and that in 1900 Providence would rectify the mistake made in 1896, and again call on them to direct the destinies of Canada. But it was not to be. In the four years from 1896 to 1900, the people _ of Canada had come to realize the success of the policy of the Liberal party in the development of their business, and in the extra profits they had gained from their business, and they saw at once the difference between the successful policy of the Liberal party and the defective policy of the Conservative party. And after the elections of 1900, the Conservative party came back to this House bereft of all its great leaders who had made that party famous, and many of their supporters met the same fate. The Liberals had a greater majority in 1900 than they had after the elections,in 1896, a testimony that the people of Canada were able to appreciate good government.
I remember that in 1900, in the town of Alexandria in my county, Sir Charles Tapper, the Hon. George E. Foster, the Hon. Hugh John Macdonald, Mr. Bergeron, Mr. APRIL 29. 1903
R. R. MacLennan, Mr. Quinn, Mr. Broder, and a half dozen other notable Conservative started a tour which they wound up in the North-west, endeavouring to electrify the people to rally to their standard. They made a great flourish of trumpets in Alexandria; they had| a street procession and a hippodrome worthy of any circus. The Liberals of Glengarry felt that they were taken by storm when this great galaxy of ability and talent invaded our town. But what was the result ? The people of Glengarry are canny Scotch and they can count the dollars well. They had lived under four-years of prosperous government, four years of careful administration which gave to the manufacturers and the consumers each their just share; four years of prosperity such as up to that time this country had never known and when the votes were counted the people of Glengarry declared that they would support the Liberal party rather than return to the policy of the Conservative party under which they had made little or no progress. Glengarry is not a manufacturing county. We have only one large manufacturing concern within the limits of the county, and I may say now that that concern does not ask for any increase in the duty. The men who control that manufacturing institution come of a stock who believe that they can stand upon their own merits, their own ability, and their own capital, and they do not ask for an increase of duty on the goods they are manufacturing. They are prepared to meet any competition in the country and they are succeeding enormously well. The people of the county of Glengarry are largely farmers and labourers. They realize full well the benefits that have been derived and are to be derived from a tariff such as has been maintained by this government. Where in the history of this Dominion has there been greater strides made during the past six years than in the industry of mixed farming and dairying in which the majority of the people of my county are engaged. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) spoke about cold storage and he took credit that the Conservative party had inaugurated this system. To hear him talk you would think that the Conservatives of Canada had invented cold storage. Why, Mr. Speaker, cold storage was in successful operation years before the Conservative party had anything to do with it. There was a perfect system of mechanical refrigeration carrying perishable products from South America and Australia and landing them in good condition in England, years before it was tried in Canada. What did the Conservative government do ? They put in a few ice boxes and called them a cold storage system, and the unfortunate people who undertook to utilize them had their goods landed in Liverpool in a rrtten and useless condition. In order to prove that this cold storage system was a good one the Conservatives bought butter at 20
cents a pound throughout the country and the result was that the butter was landed in England fit only for wool grease, that it never was put on the market and sold as butter, and that it brought only 10 cents a pound in England notwithstanding that the government paid 20 cents a pound in Canada. When the Liberal government came into power they realized that some better system must be put in operation; they realized that they must inaugurate a cold storage system commensurate with the importance of the agricultural industry, and to-day we can send our butter and fruits and all perishable articles to the old country markets and deliver them there in proper condition. There is where the present government has scored one success. The county of Glengarry consists of four townships, and is probably as small a county in area as there is in the province Ontario. That small county exported last year $1,000,000 worth of dairy products, according to the statement compiled by the secretary of the Dairymen's Association of the county. That explains the reason why the people of the county of Glengarry have such a strong regard for the present government. Nor do they believe in paying taxes that go into the pockets of two or three hundred individuals instead of paying them to build public works and promote the progress of the country as a whole. I have never yet heard any of the electors of Glengarry, whether Conservative or Liberal, say that they were not willing to pay their proper share of taxation required to properly administer and develop this country. I believe that both the labouring classes and the farmers in any part of the province of Ontario or in this Dominion are willing to pay their full share; but they do object to paying into the pockets of the manufacturers 50 or 10C| per cent taxation on the articles they consume simply because the policy of the opposition is in favour of protection in the shape of high duties. No, Mr. Speaker, protection does not mean high duties; it means protecting the interests of the masses of the people.
I do not intend to discuss the mass of figures which, during this debate, have been read and reread, iterated and reiterated, and upon which the changes have been rung so many times. As has been said, figures can be made to prove anything ; but there is one thing remarkable in the figures which have been laid before us. With all the extravagance charged against the government by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor), with all the large expenditures charged by members of the opposition, with all the large revenues which the government are charged with having taken from the people, which the opposition now call taxes, though they did not do so in the old days, there is one thing that we should remember, that is, that the present government have administered the affairs of the country, have constructed large works, have developed the

Yukon, liave paid the cost of tlie Soutli African contingents, have put tlie Intercolonial Railway on a proper business basis, and have done all this from the revenues derived from the low tariff as it exists to-day, and without any large increase in the public debt, such as their predecessors made. Looking at the ' Canada Gazette ' of April 25tli, you will see that this government have been able to do all this, and still leave the public debt within $80,000 of where they found it in the year 1897.
The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) almost shed tears over the per capita taxation imposed on the people of this country. That is something like a man who has been farming or doing business all his life, at the end of a prosperous period or at a successful turn in his business, going out and buying some more property. He has the money and is able to pay for the property. Is there any reason why such a man should be commiserated because he is obliged to pay $1,000 or $2,000 for additional property which he chooses to buy ? No. And we find that in the prosperous times which the people of Canada have been enjoying under the present government, they have been able to buy two or three times as much of the dutiable articles they required, and pay for them ; and the bank returns show that they have not only been able to do that, but have large balances to their credit in the savings banks and other monetary institutions of the country, such as we have never known under the administration of the Conservative party. A per capita tax, Mr. Speaker, is the best evidence that can be brought to show the state of prosperity of the people. If the per capita tax increases from year to year, it shows that the people of Canada are progressing and increasing their wealth, and that the factories of the country, though taxed to their utmost to provide the requirements of the people, have not been able to supply them all, and so the people have had to bring in imported goods. Such has been the prosperity of the country during the last six *or seven years under the administration of the present government. But the opposition propose to change all that. They say : No ; bring in nothing ; but because the people of Canada are prosperous to-day, because they are able to stand some more taxation, we will filch from their pockets 50 or 100 per cent for the benefit of one hundred, two hundred or three hundred of our friends.
As the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) has said, the fight is on. Let the fight be on. If the proposition of the opposition in this House is that for the sake of a few hundred manufacturers of this country the rest of the people should be taxed 50 or 100 per cent, I say let us know that the fight is on, and I am satisfied that the next time we appeal to the country the majority in this House, as it stands to-day, will be returned 40 or 50 or 100 per cent larger than it is 1 Mr. SCHELL.
to-day, if that were possible. Under Conservative rule the manufacturers of this country were continually looking to the government to assure them profits and stability of business conditions-to make enactments by which they would feel safe and secure in their business enterprises. But under the system of Hooking to Ottawa for all the efforts that should be looked for at home, the business of this country was steadily going down. While the people were simply living on one another, the exporting business of the country was not increasing as it should have done. Under the fiscal change which was brought about in 1897 by this government, the manufacturers of this country came to feel that to be successful in their business they must depend upon themselves more than on the legislation of this country, and the result has been that many of those manufacturers who were looking to the government to guarantee their profits backed by parliament, got strictly down to business and conducted their industries on business principles, as they should have done years before, with the result that they have been able to make probably higher profits under a lower tariff than' in the previous years when they were depending more on the government than on themselves. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) last night used these words :
Notwithstanding the increase in population of the country required these implements, no sane man after the statements made by the right hon. leader of the government and by the hon. Finance Minister, threatening free trade, and threatening to abolish the duties would put his money into a manufacturing industry of this kind.
The hon. gentleman evidently forgot that that statement was not in accord with the facts. He said no sane man would put his money into a business of that kind. Why, Mr. Speaker, to-day in Hamilton there is being erected a greater concern than has been in this Dominion for the manufacture of these identical articles, in tlie manufacture of which the hon. gentleman said, not twenty hours ago, no sane man would put his money. Hon. members may have noticed in the newspapers a few days ago a statement made by Major Bittenger, the United States consul, that the money of the American people was pouring into this country. What for, Mr. Speaker ? Are we to conclude it is because the Americans are. insane ? No, it is because this country to-day, under its present revenue tariff, has more possibilities for the investment of capital, more avenues for profitable trade, than are to be found in the United States. Speaking of agricultural implements, the hon. member for Leeds said further that they were not adequately protected. Well. Sir, the hon. leader (Mr. Borden) declared in Manitoba that they were. That is just a small difference of opinion between these two hon. gentlemen. However, we must not take the hon. member for Leeds too

seriously. He told us last niglit tliat lie ivas simply abusing the government. He was simply out for abuse, and evidently the facts were but a secondary consideration. It must be well known to the hon. gentleman, as it is to most members of this House, that the demand for agricultural implements was so great throughout this country that our manufacturers could not supply them. He must have known that in July of last year there was not one agricultural implement in the establishment of Frost & Wood, which was not sold ahead and that in fact that firm could not begin to fill all its orders. He must have known that the Massey-Harris people were sold out of their binders, reapers and mowers, a month before the spring trade actually opened. So great has been the progress of this country, and consequently so great have been the demands in these lines, that the calculations of the manufacturers fell short of the requirements, and it was absolutely impossible for them to furnish our farmers with the implements that they required last year, even with all the advantages which these concerns enjoy for turning out the goods. That is one reason why our farmers bought from the United States, and why our importation of agricultural implements were increased last year. Just for the same reason have our imports increased in nearly all lines of manufacture throughout the Dominion. These are facts that are well known, and which prove that at present there is no need at all for protection in this country, even to the Massey-Harris people. There is no need for further protection for the manufacturers for agricultural implements, either in Toronto or in Brantford.
So far as I am concerned, I am content to take the issues as laid down by the hon. leader of the opposition and his lieutenants I am quite satisfied that we should go before the people upon these issues, and I have no doubt that when we do, the people will decide in favour of the policy of the present administration. I know that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) like the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) spoke last night under the impression that a general election is near at hand and that this might be the last session when he would be able to make statements of any kind in this House. I believe myself that my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor) will have another opportunity before this parliamentary term closes, to indulge in his abuse of the government and to define what he and his friends mean by the word ' adequate.' I hope he will address the House in the same lines as he did last night and as his lion, leader did a few days ago, and I should ask no better issue on which to appeal to the country than the policy laid down by the hon. Minister of Finance and that proposed in opposition to it by the leader of the Liberal-Conservative party in this House.

speechtext:
It is time, Mr. Speaker, I should say a few words with regard to the speeches we have heard and particularly with regard to the budget speech made by the non. Finance Minister. I must say that I thought it hardly fair for the hon. gentleman to make the comparisons he did between the large revenue he has been handling and the small revenue received by the previous Conservative government. We all know that the comparison is not one from which the hon. gentleman can draw the conclusions he did. Take up the public accounts, and you will find that in the year 1868 our revenue was some $75,000,000 and our expenditure about the same. Then turn to 1873, when Mr. Alexander Mackenzie was head of the government, and you will find that our expenditure and revenue reached a little more than $75,000,000 each. If you take 1896, you will find there was a larger revenue and expenditure, and, if you come to the last year, still larger. And so it will be for years to come-probably for ever. Therefore, I do not think it is fair for the Finance Minister to critcise as much as he did, on the basis of a comparison of the figures of 1896 and 1902. But we cannot expect much else, for every year since 1896 we have heard such talk in this House. But we have heard more than that. I heard a gentleman who was then Mr. Laurier, now Sir Wilfrid Laurier-very well, all right-I heard that gentleman say right in my own county, in 1895, on the 5tli of September :	If you elect me to power, I
will do so and so. He had five good words to give us.' One of them was : Elect me to power and I will reduce the price of coal oil. Another was : Elect me to power and I will reduce the price of farming implements. Another :	Elect me to power and
I will reduce the price of goods generally. Another :	Elect me to power and I will
reduce the public debt. Not one of these things has come to pass yet. There was another promise which he made, which I shall not mention, for, the other day I heard you, Mr. Speaker, call an hon. gentleman to order because he had wandered beyond the subject before the chair, and I do not wish the same thing to happen to me. The present leader of the government told us at that time that it was a shame for any government to have expenditures more than from thirty-eight to forty millions a year, and he declared that if he were in power he would show that the country's affairs could be carried on for that amount. Very well, what have we seen since ? We see expenditures of forty-five, fifty and sixty millions of dollars a year. Then, that right hon. gentleman said :	If you elect me to
power I will reduce the public debt to eight or ten millions of dollars. When has he reduced that debt one cent ? Never. Instead of being reduced, it has been increased. unfortunately. In 3896 the total debt was $325,000,000, in round numbers, now

it is up to $366,000,000, an increase of $41,000,000. The net debt, which was $258,497,000 in 1896, is now $271,829,000, an increase of $13,322,000. Now, we heard the Finance Minister in all his glory laughing and joking and showing himself very glad about his big income. But what does that amount to, I would like to know ? It only means that the more money he has the more pleasure he has in counting it up and paying it out. That is all that is shown by this book that the government gave me, a book that there is no denying. It speaks for itself and for the administration. Now, looking at this matter in the right light, what would the Finance Minister do if his revenue were like that of twenty or thirty years ago, while his expenses were as high as they are now ? Where would he land ? The fact is, he gets in so much money and spends so much money and does not reduce the public debt a single cent. He talks about the surplus he has and the surplus he is going to have. We have heard a great deal about such things, and that is all there is to it. He does get a big pile of money, but where is it ? The Conservative government had surpluses in the same way, but where is the money ? All this talk about surpluses reminds me of a story I heard. A slave was in the barnyard with his master, and all at once he said : * Massa, de preacher's a-comin'.' ' I don't see him coming,' said the master. ' But he's comin all right.' ' How do you know ?' ' Why, don't you see de chickens flying.' The Minister of Finance speaks of the big income he is receiving and is to receive, but what is it all for ? It is to hoodwink the people over the next election ? We have heard such talk over and over until I have got tired of it-there is nothing in it.
I hear a great many of my friends on both sides of the House talk about protection. But I would like more than talk- I would like to have some practice of protection. We talk about the American people, how industrious, how intelligent they are. Knowing them as I do, I say the same. But why is it they have become such a great nation ? It is all on account of protection. What were they up to in 1776 ? They were a colony, working hard for a living, and making no headway. But after they threw off the yoke, they started right up, they established protection, and practiced it.
Now, here we are, talking about our American friends being so intelligent. We talk about what they do, and yet we do not follow their example. After praising them so much, why should we not follow their example ? I think they deserve to be praised. We hear a great deal of talk in this House about Air. Chamberlain, Air. Chamberlain ; we hear his name mentioned three or four times too often. Air. Chamberlain may be a very good fellow, indeed I think he is a little too good. We have given him $2,648,495 last year under the preferential Mr. MORIN.
trade arrangement. I do not think that pays at all. I would sooner say more about Air. Chamberlain and give him less money. We are the ones to be protected first-that is my doctrine, anyway. But some of our friends have a great deal to say about Air. Chamberlain, and yet they do not want to look after themselves.
Now I would like to say a few words about the government's intention to go back to Washington. Some years ago we voted $30,000 to pay their trip to Washington ; I suppose pretty soon we will be called upon to vote another sum to pay another trip. Now I wish to give the government a little advice. They talk about going to Washington to make a treaty in regard to the Alaska boundary. I would be very glad if they would stay at home. They must know very well what the result was some four years ago. Air. Speaker, let us look at the facts of history, and you will understand how little the United States are willing to give ns. After the treaty of 1784 the boundary line was run from the St. Lawrence river to Aladawanpec Point in the state of Alaine. Well, two years after that, our American friends were not willing to live up to that treaty, they wanted to gobble up a big portion of what now forms the state of Maine. About the same time another treaty was made according to which the line was to be drawn from the head of Lake Superior to Puget Sound. What did they do later on, in 1813 ? They took a strip of land from us one hundred and fifty miles wide from Du-ulth to Rainy River, and thence to Puget Sound. Then in 1848 or 1849 they were still unsatisfied, and they took another strip of land from us along the St. John river. True, it is not worth much, there are scarcely any settlers on it. These facts show you what we can expect from them. I have resided in that country for thirty-five years, and I have had many discussions with their people in regard to these questions. They are always willing and ready to take, but they are never willing to give. They are not even willing to give what they ought to give, and what does not belong to them. Tf our government go down to Washington again, the only result will be that they will spend the public money, and the Americans will laugh at them as they did at the last meeting. I spent two months last summer down in the States, and I had talks with congressmen. judges and lawyers on public questions. and they just made fun of us Canadians. They say :	You Canadians come
over here expecting to get a strip of land away from us, but that is all in your eye. Aly advice to this government is to stay where you are. That is all I have to say for the present.

speechtext:
I feel some delicacy in taking part in this debate on account of the deep interest which is manifested by members of this House, and the large numbers present to listen to

the discussion. It is very encouraging to hon. members who wish to participate in this debate to find the House so full, indeed I may say overflowing, as it should be at this particular time. This is a time when the finances of the country are in a particularly good shape, everything is buoyant, and under these circumstances we could expect nothing else but that the House should be well attended during the budget debate.
April 16th, 1903, will be memorable in the annals of this country. It wag on that day that the hon. the Minister of Finance moved the following resolution :
That the House resolve itself into Committee to consider of the Ways and Means for raising the Supply to be granted to His Majesty.
This resolution whilst moved by finance ministers for many years, gave added pleasure to the representatives in this House from the remarks which followed on that particular occasion. As loyal representatives of the people we are pleased to accede to the wishes of the advisers of His Majesty, and while it is our privilege to criticise the expenditure, we do so with a knowledge of the facts, as recorded- in the public documents and as told us by the hon. the Finance Minister, and shown by the abundant trade of the country.
Perhaps before I go further in the remarks which I propose to offer to this House, I may refer to a statement made by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Morin), who seems to have forgotten the facts. He said that the Liberals in opposition had promised that if they got into power the duty would be taken off coal oil, and that they had not done so. I beg to assure him that the duty has been taken off coal oil. He also said that this government promised to reduce the public debt. Well, we have the assurance of the Finance Minister that the indebtedness which has been incurred by this government will be very materially reduced, and nearly wiped out next year. The budget shows clearly that the system of taxation inaugurated by the present government in 1897 was a good one. It has made for every stability, that under its benign influence, the trade and prosperity of the country has expanded by leaps and bounds.
The revenue for 1900-01 was	$52,514,701
"	" 1901-02	"	 58,050,790
Net increase	$ 5,536,088
Mr. Speaker, this is a remarkable showing. Our revenue has increased to such proportions that it is a matter of rejoicing to every true and loyal Canadian, because of propositions with which we are confronted in the building up of this vast country. But, Mr. Speaker, although the net increase of last year was very large, the best is yet to come, and the hon. minister informs us that the year closing June 30th, 1903. will be much better, indeed far ahead of the best we have ever witnessed, with the extraordinary estimated surplus of $13,350,000.
We are speaking of the present, but I would remind the House that this state of affairs, this growing time has existed since this government has been in power.
The revenue since 1896 has been as follows :-
1896		$36,618,591
1897		 37,829,778
1898		 40,555,238
1899		 46,741,250
1900		 51,029,994
1901		 52,514,701
1902		 58,050,790
I claim it is a remarkable showing for the present government that has been so much belied. If you will look over the statement of revenue as presented during the years which preceded 1896 you will find that the revenue was almost stationary, that it did not increase at all, that as soon as this government; took hold the increase became permanent and rapid, and that it went up from $36,000,000 in 1896 to $58,000,000 in 1002. The opponents of this government are apt to belittle efforts to promote trade and commerce and to attribute the growth of Canada's trade to everything and anything else than the present administration. They point to the increased trade of all the world, and then go so far as to say that if there has been prosperity it Is because we adopted the protective plank of their platform. If shown different by the fact of so many items being put on the free list and radical cuts made on scores of dutiable goods they then say : It must be a miracle for none but Conservatives could have accomplished so much. I am reminded of a story of a lawyer who was examining an expert witness to ascertain if he exactly understood what a miracle was. The lawyer said to him ; Suppose you find yourself in a window of that twelfth story building opposite and the next moment you fall to the pavement and find yourself uninjured-what would you call that ? The witness said : I would call that an accident. Well, that *was not just the answer that the lawyer expected and he repeated the question. He asked him, if a second time, he found himself uninjured what he would call that. The witness said ; I would call that a coincidence. He was getting the matter down pretty fine but the lawyer repeated the question, and said : Suppose you should find yourself upon the pavement a third time uninjured, what would you call that ? The witness replied : I would, call it a habit. These distinctions are very fine. It was purely accidental that this government was able to get into office and conduct affairs, it was coincidence that they continued to do so and it is now becoming a habit. They acknowledge first, second and third, and finally they say it must be a miracle as such a thing was never known or seen for a Liberal government or party in Canada being able to properly direct the affairs of the country. People like these must surely be blind for we have the largest surplus-except one-that

Canada has ever known and that was two years since, and under Liberal rule. The Finance Minister assures us that the revenue for the ensuing year will he far larger and that he exjiects the revenue for this year, 1902-03, to reach the handsome total of $65,000,000.
Amongst the causes which have contributed to this remarkable state of affairs must be counted the just, and wise expenditure and administration of the departments. The Post Office Department is one, which, notwithstanding the efforts of the opposition to explain away its very wise administration by the Postmaster General, makes a record. They cannot conceive that the best and most modern methods have been adopted and abuses done away with. And it is entirely beyond their conception how a deficit of $700,000 in 1896 was reduced to a deficit of $105,000 in 1901-2 ; nor do they seem to realize that the postal services were extended and enlarged during that period. The number of post offices has increased as follows
1896		 9,103
1897		 9,191
1898		 9,282
1899		 9,420
1900		 9,627
1901		 9,834
1902		 9,958
An increase of 855 post offices during the seven years of Liberal rule. What does this mean ? It means an increase in the expenditure of the department and if anything could account for an Increase in the expenditure I think it is this statement which I have just read showing the extensions which have been made in the post office service. It costs money to open new post offices. There is a matter of public interest to which I am sure, in due time, the Postmaster General will direct his attention : It is the matter of free rural deliveries. I will admit that the conditions existing in this country on account of its great extent and sparse settlements are not ideal ones. But there are some of the older settled portions of the country where it might well be introduced. It will be acceded that there has been no time in the world's history when enlightened governments have made such efforts to ameliorate the conditions of life which contribute and conduce to the happiness of the people as in the present. And our government, I am sure, will not be behind in matters which are so vital to the welfare of the great farming community. I can speak with some authority on this matter, as I come from a constituency where the greater number of our people are farmers. The recent census taken in Canada, as well as that in the United States, go far to show that city life has its attractions over the young people in the rural districts of the country. And that wherever the great centres of population are increasing the country portions are lessened in population. In my opinion the post offices, and telephones, are to play an important part in making the lot of the farmer more congenial. And if, as is expected, the farmer has his free mail delivery, bringing his letters and daily papers with news of the outside world, a telephone in his house with which he can communicate with his neighbours and friends, and even with the more distant cities and great markets, the life of the farmer would take on a different aspect. But on all sides it was admitted that when the present government came into power the road was in an impoverished condition. All this has been changed, and under the able management of its present Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) it is no more a reproach, and I have been informed by commercial travellers and tourists from foreign countries that there is not a more comfortable and up-to-date railway in Canada today. Living in Ontario, to which province the road does not extend, it was always very difficult for me to understand how a railway running through the old settled provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Quebec, having a live business population, rich in natural resources, and carrying freight to all our great seaports of the Atlantic, did not pay. The present minister undertook to extend the road to Montreal, the great eastern inland seaport in Canada, and then a change occurred. And if the surplus has been small for some years of his administration this fact coupled with efficiency and economical management accounts for the better and changed condition of the road. Tf by the extension of the Intercolonial Railway to Montreal such results have been accomplished is it not fair to, at least, hope, that if the Intercolonial Railway were extended further west, to the great lakes, where it could enjoy a share of the great traffic which comes from our boundless wheat fields, greater results would follow. In connection with the very great interest which the public are taking in railways which will span the Canadian portion of this continent, one proposition is that the government should extend the track of the intercolonial Railway at least to Winnipeg and allow any railway wanting access to the western country from the east to have wheelage rights over this government road-

That produce will then be delivered to its destination in as good order as when shipped.
By this means our producers have the advantage of shipping their products at various points and having it delivered in perfect condition either for the local trade or for export. What this means in the case of butter and cheese and eggs and other perishable products, it is hardly necessary to tell our farmers.
Coming to the question of public debt, not only have we a surplus revenue, but we are reducing our public debt, which is practical evidence that the surplus is a real one. Although we have been compelled to incur a large expenditure in order to meet the needs of the country-an expenditure which is perfectly justifiable-it is very gratifying to have our Finance Minister announce that practically all the additions made to the public debt by this government would be wiped out in another year, and that the net debt of our population will be $48 per head, as compared with $50 per head in 1896. He also stated that there will be loans maturing in. Canada to the amount of $2,800,000, which are now bearing 4 per cent interest and that these loans will be refloated at 34 per cent. I hope that the people of this country will subscribe to the new loan to be voted in payment of our maturing obligations. I believe that the practice of floating government loans among the people of this country is one that should be encouraged. I think it w'ould tend to increase a man's patriotism to know that he is holding a $100 or a $500 or a $1,000 bond of this government. What safer security can he have ? If everything else should go to ruin, we still have the country left, we still have the land, and we still have ample guarantee for our government bonds. There can be no security so safe as a government loan, and the people of this country might very well invest some of the $60,000,000 which they have in the Government Post Office Savings Banks in their own national securities. For these reasons I believe that a popular loan in this country would be one issued by the government of a moderate amount, bearing interest of three and a half per cent, say for twenty years, and in denominations of $100 or $500. Such a loan would encourage national sentiment. I am a great believer in allowing our people all the privileges we can give them,

It is gratifying to note the abundant prosperity existing throughout Canada. It would be idle to contend that the government has created all this prosperity. But is it not fair to concede some credit to the government ? Former governments sought to impress the people in a general way with the idea that the country could not do very well without them and that it would certainly go to ruin under Liberal rule. But what is the condition to-day. Our railways are not able to handle with any degree of despatch the freight that is offering. And indeed, during many months, they have been paralyzed and conjested with traffic. I saw last night a report in one of our newspapers-the Toronto ' World,' I think it was -that the railways were not able to handle the traffic, that there were over five hundred cars in the Toronto yards waiting to be unloaded. Of course, that might be the fault of the railways not having enough labour to take care of the freight. But the same is true all over the country. I have seen it stated, time and time again, in the newspapers of the day, that the railways have plenty to keep them busy. Indeed, I was told recently by a man from the west that even If there were no crop in the west this year there was sufficient grain in the country, there were enough people going up and sufficient freight being carried to supply them, to keep the railways fully employed. This is the condition of affairs in relation to the railways, which are the pulse of the country. Banks have been doing an enormous business and showing fine yearly statements of earnings, and their record is that the deposits are larger than ever before in the history of the country. The demand for government currency has been abnormal, reaching $30,000,000, or perhaps $35,000,000 per year. Factories have sprung into existence everywhere, and the general testimony is that many of them have more orders than they can complete for months to come. Large industries employing thousands of men, especially in iron and coal, which are the great staple productions, have been established. The farmers of this great Dominion have grown wealthy, and there is no class of the community but have improved their earnings. It is needless for me to speak of the prosperity of other classes. But I do say that these conditions exist in my own section of the country. Everything is thoroughly prosperous, and the prospects of all never were so hopeful. If we consult the trade returns, we find that the total trade of the country has increased by $200,000,000 since 1895, or over $28,000,000 per year on the average. And of this increase about half was in the export trade, which is of the greatest benefit to the country. I wish particularly to congratulate the gov-

eminent on its proposal to place a surtax on German goods. The press throughout the country have approved of the government's action, particularly because of its departure from antiquated methods. I notice by the cable reports that the press of outside countries has commented favourably on the government's policy. If we are to believe the reports of many writers on trade relations, the coming years will witness a great struggle for commercial supremacy, and the action of Germany, which provoked our government to reprisals, may indicate in some measure the correctness of this view, and shows that we must take care of ourselves. No doubt, this government will be able and always willing to take care of the trade of Canada. It is satisfactory to observe the buoyancy of the revenue derived from customs duties. For, after all, this is the chief source of taxation. Though we pay for the support of government in other ways, the chief source of the government's revenue is the customs. One can idealize and theorize on a tariff and can frame a tariff in his mind which, to all intents and purposes, will be a perfect one. But it is a difficult thing to enter practically into the trade of the country and collect a revenue from the vast number of articles which are brought in and, at the same time, not materially injure or oppress any interest. Now, in a general way, I think this government has done this, and that Canada never had a tariff which could meet all the requirements of the people so well. It is not correct to say that it is a perfect tariff, but it has done the greatest good to the greatest number, and that is right. There are inequalities iu the tariff, as we must all admit, and some of these inequalities I see exemplified in the affairs of some people in my own riding. But I am sure the government will take these things into account when the proper time comes for the readjustment of the tariff. It is not fair to say that this government has vacillated and has no policy. Our opponents have stated over and over again that their policy lias been adopted. But, to my mind at least, a tariff is largely a compromise, and I repeat again that the task of harmonizing the various interests of the country has been well performed by this government. In view of what I have said, and of a good deal more that I might say, and in view of the progress of the country, I cannot support the amendment of the leader of the opposition. He asks us to declare that the present tariff is unsatisfactory. I do not believe that it is unsatisfactory ; I believe it is satisfactory ; that it has, in a great measure, created prospei'ity in the country. I presume I have the right to my opinion, and that is my opinion-that the present tariff has in great measure contributed to the success and welfare of the Dominion.
