The Minister of Finance, in his budget speech, made reference to Germany and to the German tariff and he read the correspondence which took place between this government and Lord Strathcona, and between this government and the Imperial German Consul. Let me say, Sir, that in the session of 1901, I asked for any correspondence which had passed between the parliament of the Dominion or the British government, or the government of Germany with reference to this question. At that time demands were being made upon this government by boards of trade throughout Canada, asking them to do something in the line of passing retaliatory legislation if necessary in order to off-set the humiliating position in which Germany had, placed Canada. The Prime Minister replied in answer to my question :	That there was no
correspondence on the question to be brought down. Well, Sir, in looking over the correspondence which has now been placed before the House I find that on June 27th, 1898, Lord Strathcona sent a cable to the Minister of Trade and Commerce to this effect :	Shall I enter protest against Germany's action; and lie followed that cable up with a letter. Let me point out to the House the very dilatory manner in which the Canadian government treated this very 65i
important question. This cable was on June 27, 1898, and on August 2, of that year the Department of Trade and Commerce replied, thanking Lord Strathcona for his prompt action in connection with the matter, but giving him no further instructions whatever. That is the only letter so far as I am able to discover in this correspondence, which passed between the government and any party or parties in respect to this question until the Prime Minister took the matter up with the German Imperial Consul at Montreal, November, 1901. Lord Strathcona, on September 17, 1899, asked of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to be favoured with instructions by the govenynent on this subject, and remarkably strange to say the Canadian government gave no reply to that letter. Again on May 8, 1901, Lord Strathcona wrote to the Minister of Trade and Commerce telling what lie was doing and adding :	I trust it will meet with the approval of the government. As in the former case Lord Strathcona received no reply or acknowledgment to this letter. Again on August 1, 1901, Lord Strathcona addressed a letter to this government which was treated in the like manner, and that brings us down to the correspondence of November 4, 1901, in which the Prime Minister asked the German Imperial Consul to call upon him in order that they might discuss the matter. What I claim, Sir, is, that the correspondence which was then in the hands of the government should have been brought down when we asked for it. The government treated the correspondence as though it were of a serious nature, but there was nothing secret or private about it. In the session of 1902 my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) again asked for this correspondence and it was again refused. Ii is very easily seen from the correspondence itself that it is of a comparatively trifling character, and my only explanation as to why the government refused to bring it before the House is, that they were ashamed to show how little attention they had given to this German business. It is only when we on this side of the House moved in the matter and forced the hands of the government that they really took the question up seriously. However that may be, I am prepared to endorse the action of the government in the stand they have taken towards Germany. I take no stock whatever in the attitude of Germany or the German press towards us. In discussing this question with shippers of grain and cereals in this country, since the Minister of Finance brought this question to an issue, they have assured me that Germany has already done all she can do against Canada.
If Germany or any other country institutes against this country a tariff which is almost prohibitive, what difference does it make how much they increase that tariff- whether they double or treble it ? Whatever it is, it cuts us out of the German mar-

ket; and I think we can afford to let other countries know that on fiscal questions we are independent and can do as we desire, though being a dependency of Great Britain. The answer that I would give to Germany, if she continues to attack us, is simply this : Why should the German tariff on our products be more than it is upon the products of the United States ? That is a simple way of putting the case, and I venture to say that there is no answer to it. We need not go into a discussion of the Belgian and German treaties or favoured-nation treatment. This country imports more proportionately from Germany than the United States, and our tariff is very much lower than the tariff of the United States. Therefore, I think our government have taken the right stand, and I do not anticipate any further legislation from Germany, of a character that will hurt us. 1 really cannot understand the attitude of Germany. We are on a par with the United States in everything. Does Germany choose to treat Canada in this way because it is a dependency of Great Britain ? Is it because of the easy-going methods of the British people on trade matters that Germany undertakes to discriminate against us in this way ? At any rate, I feel that we are on safe ground, and I am pleased at the stand the government have taken in regard to the matter.
I do not propose at this stage to discuss the very important question of protection which has been so much discussed in this House. I hope I shall have an opportunity at a later date to express my views on the very important subject. I may say, however, that I shall heartily support the amendment which has been placed before the House by the hon. leader of the opposition.
I would like, however, for a few moments to take up the time of the House in regard to the question of preferential trade. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that a year ago we had a discussion in reference to the invitation which was sent to the government to attend the coronation ceremonies and the colonial conference in London. We on this side of the House expressed the opinion that the government had replied to that invitation in a way that was entirely unwarranted. The invitation stated that it was desirable that the colonial conference should discuss three matters :	Political
relations existing within the empire, the question of defence, and the question of commercial relations. The reply of the government to this invitation stated that the only question which gave promise of useful discussion was that of commercial relations. We on this side of the House took the position that the government should go to the conference with an open mind, willing to discuss any question which might come before it. At the bottom of their reply to the invitation the government did say that they would be willing to discuss any question

which came up, but it did not appear to me that that statement qualified their main position to any great extent. The position I take in regard to Canada not being able to secure from Great Britain a preference on our cereals, which I think we should have secured under the grain tax, was due to our attitude on the subject of defence. Hon. members will know in regard to this important question what my views are, as I put them on record last session and they are not too radical. As this question has not been considered to any great extent since the abolition of the war tax on grain in Great Britain, I would like to draw the attention of the House to the very serious way in which the Secretary of State for the Colonies, Mr. Chamberlain, discussed the question of imperial defence at the colonial conference. As I want to place his views before the House, I will take the liberty of reading what he said on the subject in his opening address :
As regards imperial defence, I propose to lay before you, for your information, a paper which will show the comparative amount of the ordinary naval and military expenditure of the United Kingdom and of the different self-governing colonies. You will find that in the case of the United Kingdom the cost of our armaments has enormously increased since 1897. That increase is not entirely due to our initiative, but it is forced upon us by the action of other powers who have made great advances, especially in connection with the navy, which we have found it to be our duty and necessity to equal. But the net result is extraordinary. At the present moment the estimates for the present year for naval and military expenditure in the United Kingdom-not including the extraordinary war expenses, but the normal estimates-Involve an expenditure per head of the population of the United Kingdom of 29 shillings 3d.-29s. 3d. per head per annum.

In New South Wales-I have not the figures for the Commonwealth as a whole, but I am giving those as illustrations-and I find that in New Sofith Wales the expenditure is 3 shillings 5d.; in Victoria, 3 shillings 3d.; in New Zealand, 3 shillings 4d.; and in the Cape and Natal, I think it is between two shillings and three shillings. Now, no one, I think, will pretend that that is a fair distribution of the burdens of the empire. No one will believe that the United Kingdom can, for all time, make this inordinate sacrifice. While the colonies were young and poor, in the first place they did not offer anything like the same temptation to the ambitions of others, and, in the second place, they were clearly incapable of providing large sums for their own defence, and therefore it was perfectly right and natural that the mother country should undertake the protection of her children. But now that the colonies are rich and powerful, that every day they are growing by leaps and bounds, their material prosperity promises to rival that of the United Kingdom itself, and I think it is incon-

In his budget speech in 1898, the lion. Minister of Finance referred to it as a measure of tariff reform and the hon. Minister of the Interior, in the House in 1901, said :
When we give preference, if it is to he at any one's expense, it is at the expense of the manufacturer and the workingman of Canada. We go a little further, and say that it is the policy of the Liberal party of Canada to reduce the duties and to remove to some extent the burden of the excessive tariff which was imposed on imported goods by the late Conservative government.
These are the views of two of the ministers of this government. The right hon. Prime Minister, however, said something different. In Interviews and speeches in 1897, he said :
I have too great a belief in British common sense to think that they will do any such thing

He was referring to the adoption of protection by Great Britain.
What we have done in the way of tariff preference, we have done out of gratitude to England.
Therefore it can easily be seen that this government were using this preferential tariff as a sort of a political weapon which could cut any way they chose.
But when we come down to the present session, we do not see in the reply by the right hon. First Minister to the speech from the Throne any reference to the scheme which he propounded at that colonial conference with reference to a Canadian naval force. On the contrary, the government have studiously avoided any reference to that important question, which was discussed at the conference. I do not find that the hon. Minister of Finance, in his speech on the budget, made any reference whatever to this statement which was made at the colonial conference, but he held out the hope to the country that when the British budget came down, we would find in it a return for what wo gave in the shape of a preference. The British budget has since been brought down; and I am at a loss to know how the Minister of Finance could have expected, after what I may term the bungling way in which this question has been treated, any such preference from Great Britain as he anticipated. The British people, realizing what had taken place at the conference and the vacillating way in which the question of defence has been treated, knowing that we were the only country that had given a preference and had been asking a preference in return, feeling that we had not assumed the obligation which we ought to have assumed, hearing of our overflowing treasury yet, knowing that we were not ready to do anything on behalf of the British navy, or the establishment of a navy of our own they swept the whole thing out of existence and thus declared that they would do no more. When you think of the teeming thousands coming into Mr. KEMP.
this country from the United States, is it not easy to see that one of the greatest ben-fits this country could have offered to these Americans who, we hope will become good Canadians, would have been to say to them: You can get a preference of from four to five cents a bushel on your grain grown in Canada. That would have satisfied them and would have had a good effect upon their minds in regard to the advantage of living in this country. But, what do we find ? For instance, what do we find to be the position the Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has taken in regard to this question ? He has coined a phrase, and expects to escape under it. I think it runs,
1 Canada must keep free from the vortex of European militiarism.' I do not think that, when the question is sifted to the bottom, that phrase will be accepted in place of what the government should have done by the people of this country. I do not think there was any danger to any course of a magnanimous character that we might adopt with regard to this question of defence, that would lead us into the vertex of militarism. Why could we not have said something of an encouraging character to the British people, why could not our representatives have been resourceful enough to have suggested some way whereby our own vessels might relieve to some extent the British war vessels that patrol our coasts and protect our commerce ? We shall be willing to face these responsibilities that all other nations must face, and I claim that we are occupying a humiliating position, a position which we cannot very long occupy, and which the British people have stated very plainly, through Mr. Chamberlain, that we cannot expect to occupy in not being willing to face the responsibility and perform this duty. We do not want the British taxpayers to protect us. We are in the same position as the most helpless, most significant British colony. We might have retained all our rights and yet have done something to satisfy the British people. I repeat that I am surprised that the Finance Minister expected to get any consideration when the British budget was brought down. Various unfavourable comments have been made on our attitude by the British press. Sir William Vernon Hareourt has said in speaking on the recent British Budget
The colonies ought to contribute to the navy. No sober-minded man could justify the enormous expenditure of the government.
So, we know what the feeling is in regard to this matter in Great Britain. But what is to be done in regard to this preference ? The government gave it as a measure of tariff reform and as a tribute of gratitude to the mother country. But when the Minister of Finance, the other day, brought in his budget, he almost repeated the words which were in the memorandum ! laid before the conference. He said

But, putting aside other considerations, it the British government and people do not show any appreciation of the value of the preference, then, so far as the British government and the people are concerned, they cannot complain if we see fit to modify or change that preferential tariff.
I was in the House when the hon. gentleman uttered those words, and nearly every hon. gentleman on the other side applauded. Is not this a notable thing when we remember that when the preference was introduced in 1897, hon. gentlemen opposite sang the National Anthem. Now we see that the government is in a most peculiar and erratic position, an inconsistent position, with regard to this matter. They have charged us with huckstering in regard to our policy on the preference. What have they been doing ? Huckstering of the very worst kind. When, from time to time, we have criticised this kind of a preference, and condemned the government for bringing it into effect, they have sought to meet us with the challenge : Move a resolution to do away with it. Our reply has been that it was not our affair. We have criticised it on what we consider a sound basis. What we have always advocated is what we call a mutual preference throughout the empire, and nothing short of that would be satisfactory. I contend that the government made a mistake when they did not proceed along the lines proposed by the opposition in this House. We are anxious to know what their policy is. Now is the time to state it. The Minister of Finance has excused himself for not changing the tariff this year. One of his excuses was the hope of a British preference to be announced in the British budget. We now have the British budget before us and know where we are. Now we ask, and reasonably ask, what the policy of the government is going to be in regard to this important matter. We have finished, I trust, in sending delegations of this character to Great Britain. In 1897 we sent a delegation to attend the Jubilee, and again, in 1902, we sent a delegation to the coronation. So far as I am concerned I should be ashamed to face the British nation or to go to Great Britain at the present time, after what we have done. I hope the day is not far distant when we shall take up t>.ifi question Of defence and decide what our po'ricy is to be. We have had enough frivolity in regard to the lavish way in which our statesmen have been entertained on the other side of the water. We have had enough cou-t dresses; we have had enough cocked ha'-g; we have had enough garden parties; we have had enough excursions; we have hai enough reviews; we have had enough afte,. dinner speeches; we have had enough Cobde. club medals. Let us now get down to our serious duties ; let us discharge our obligations

speakeroldname: Mr. W. A. GALLIHER (Yale and Cariboo).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join the speakers who have preceded me on this side of the House in congratulating the hon. Minister of Finance and his colleagues upon the splendid showing detailed in the budget speech so ably delivered by that hon. gentleman, a showing which, I believe, has never been equalled in the history of Canada. It must be a source of gratification to every Canadian to know that his country is in such a prosperous condition as it is, to know that our finances are being ably administered by the Finance Minister and that those finances are in a healthy condition. I know that hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House are wont to attribute much of the prosperity Canada is enjoying at the present time to a beneficient Providence. We on this side of the House equally recognize that Providence has been kind to Canada. But while we recognize this, we claim and I think we justly claim, that Canada should feel herself fortunate in having an administration at the helm capable of turning these beneficient gifts of Providence to good account. Now, I listened with considerable pleasure to the speech of tlie Finance Minister. I followed him closely throughout his speech, and I may say I listened to it with considerable pride. However, there was one thing that I did not like. It seems there is no cup so replete with sweetness that some person may not find therein a little bitterness. The sweetness lasted, so far as the people I represent are concerned, pretty nearly until the end of the minister's speech. The little bitterness that crept in came when the minister dealt with the question of adjusting the tariff on lead products. We were told that the government could not see their way clear to grant the request that had been made to them by the silver lead miners of British Columbia.
Now I may say that in British Columbia the people have always been an uncomplaining people. I have) lived there myself for the past seven years, and before that I had lived for some fifteen years in the city of AYinnipeg and west of that towards the coast, and I am well acquainted with the western people. We have always paid taxes in British Columbia by way of duty, either directly or indirectly, on every product that was brought into that country. We pay a duty direct or indirect on all we consume, on all we wear, on all our mining machinery that is not manufactured in Canada, practically on all our mining supplies; and yet I do not think that this government or any other government has ever heard any serious complaint from British Columbia on that score. But when the conditions of lead mining became such that it absolutely required assistance in some way, tfien the people of British Columbia came to this parliament. Delegations waited upon the govern-

ment, and their representatives in parliament have urged their cause. We hoped therefore that so far as lead was concerned there would he a readjustment of the tariff.
Now let me contrast the duties on lead with the duties on other products which we have to buy in British Columbia. I think I am safe in saying that probably the duties will average nearly 30 per cent on the articles that we consume and use in daily life in British Columbia. In regard to lead, let me first take the article of pig lead. We find that on pig lead there is a duty of 15 per cent; with the preference of 33& per cent deducted from all lead sent from London, that duty amounts to 10 per cent. Now probably every member in the House knows what pig lead is, but as possibly some one may not, I will explain that the lead ore is first smelted, and with the lead silver is frequently found. The smelted product of lead ore is called bullion. That bullion is then sent to the refinery where it is desilverized, and assumes the form of pig lead. Now note that the tariff of 15 per cent is levied on lead which has reached that state; and as I said before, with the preference of only 10 per cent as against London. Now we go further and take up the question of corroded lead, or what is known as white lead. Now note the anomaly. On corroded lead, which is lead advanced a further stage, the duty is only 5 per cent. Taking that fact into consideration, it is no wonder that we have no lead corroding works in Canada. That duty of 5 per cent would also have to be reduced by one-third in case the corroded lead came from England.
Now what is our position to-day ? Canada is consuming to-day of lead products in various forms, such as sheet lead, white lead, shot and corroded leads, something in the neighbourhood of 15,000 tons. This consumption is rapidly increasing from year to year, and in view of the great immigration coming into Canada at the present time it is certain to increase very rapidly in the future. Therefore we should not be surprised to find that within a very few years Canada! may be using 20,000 to 25,000 tons of lead in all forms. We have in British Columbia, particularly in tho district I represent-indeed I think I represent most all the silver lead mining interests in Canada, certainly all those in British Columbia-we have there at the present time mines capable of producing 30,000 tons of lead, and even more. As I have already said, Canada is consuming at the present time some
15.000	tons. Now how much of that lead is produced in British Columbia ? About
4.000	tons, or at the outside, 5,000 tons. You may/ ask me how that happens. The reason is that we are thrown into competition with Mexican lead. As I have shown, we are protected by no existing duty that is of any practical benefit to the mine owner or the producer; certainly the existing duty

is no benefit to the producer of lead as it stands to-day. Therefore we are thrown into competition with lead that is sent in from the United States, although not by any means produced in that country. But the United States have what is called a bonding privilege with Mexico, where there are large lead mines and where a great quantity of lead is mined. "That Mexican lead is sent into the United States in bond, is treated by United States manufacturers in bond, and then shipped out of the United States into Canada. That lead is very cheaply produced. The cost of labour employed in producing that lead is only 50 cents a day. I understand the miners are paid 50 cents in the Mexican mines. Against that we have to pay our miners $3.50 a day. You can readily see under these circumstances that we cannot possibly compete with the Mexican lead, unless some protection is afforded our miners in one way or another. If that lead is sent to London, or if Spanish lead is sent to London and refined there, and then sent out to Canada, that cheap lead comes in here with this preference deducted from the duty of 15 per cent on pig lead and 5 per cent on corroded lead.
Now, I wish for a moment to conti'ast the conditions of the United States miner and the Canadian miner of lead. For that purpose, I will take one of the western states, which hasi the greatetet lead [DOT]producing' camp in the world, the Cordellaines, in the state of Idaho, which is some 200 or 300 miles south of us. I select that because the conditions there are very similar to the conditions in British Columbia, where we are operating our mines. I find that in the United States at the present time the mine owner receives for his lead in ore $3.90 per hundred. In Canada I find that the mine owner receives for his lead in ore $1.90 per hundred. That is based upon this : We receive and are settled with on the basis of the London price. The price of lead on the London market varies from time to time, varies probably every day, or few days, a few points, but at the present time the London price is $2.90 per hundred pounds. The mine owner receives only $1.90, the other dollar being taken for freight, treatment and what are called marketing charges. So that, as contrasted with the mine owner hi the United States who receives $3.90, the mine owner in Canada, 200 or 300 miles north of him, receives only $l.ol. Now, taking pig lead in the New Y>rk market, we find that at present the pi'ice is about $4.37 per hundred. In Montreal they buy pig lead (not the United states pig lead), and the price of pig pad in Montreal is $3.07 per hundred. 7 am quoting these figures to come to tie point that I do not see why the chard' to the Canadian consumer of mixed paints should be as much as the charge t' tlle American consumer of mixed paints and yet we find that such is

tlie case. Pig lead in New York is worth $4.37 and in Montreal $3.07. Then, we find that corroded lead in New York is worth $4.75 per hundred and in Montreal $3.75 per hundred, but when it comes down to mixed paints we find that they are quoted in both countries at about $6 per hundred. One thing is sure, that the mine owner does not get the benefit of that. Why when there is such a difference in the price of pig lead and the price of corroded lead in Montreal and in New York the price of mixed paints is the same, is something that is difficult to understand. When it is mixed in with the oil and becomes mixed paint we find that, although the American paint mixer has to pay much more for the corroded lead that is used in the mixing of the paint than does the paint mixer in Montreal, practically the consumer in the United States pays the same as the consumer in Canada. This is something the government might look into.
I wish to place before the government and the House the importance of this lead industry in British Columbia, to show what it was when the conditions were favourable to mining operations there and to contrast the conditions then with the conditions today and with the conditions that have prevailed for some little time. These figures have been carefully compiled toy men who made it their special business to arrive at the figures in order to be able to present them to the government when they came here as accredited delegates from British Columbia. There has been invested in silver lead mines in that district over $20,000,000. That is the actual purchase price of the mines. It does not include any stock dealings or anything of that kind ; it is the actual purchase price of the mines and money expended in developing these mines. In connection with that, there have been railway and steamship lines built, and they were built very largely for the purpose of conveying these ores, because there were practically no other industries in certain parts of the silver lead mining district. There has been expended in that direction by the Great Northern Railway Company some $3,000,000. There has Been expended by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company for a similar purpose some $10,000,000. In Slocan district, which is entirely dependent on silver lead mining, we find that in the various mining camps and small towns the assessed value! of improved property amounts to about $1,750,000. The assessed value of the city of Nelson, outside of that amount, is placed at about $2,500,000. There has been invested in smelters for the reduction of these lead ores some $750,000 or $1,000,000, this investment being represented by the smelters at Pilot Bay, at the city of Nelson and at Trail. I will take the year 1900. because in that year the mines were working under favourable conditions and were working to their normal capacity. In that year,
while working to their normal capacity, these lead mines gave employment to 2,500 miners. This does not include men who might be employed in cutting trails or in cutting wood in connection with these mines, but actual miners, and the wages paid to these miners amounted to about $2,750,000 in that year. The value of the ores shipped from these mines in 1900 was about $5,000,000. These mines were supporting a population of some 20,000 people, I may say, almost absolutely dependent on the successful operation of the mines. Take the conditions two years later, and what do we find ? We find that the value of the ores shipped from these mines had dropped from $5,000,000 to $1,154,000. We find that the population of
20,000	people that were being supported by these mines had dwindled to some 10,090 people, and that number to-day is greatly decreasing. We find that the 2,500 men who were employed in 1900, when conditions were favourable, are reduced to 500 men, and consequently, instead of having 2,500 men working in our silver lead mines, as in 1900, we have 500 men. Instead of having $2,-
750,000	expenditure in the shape of wages, we have now only about $500,900. You will readily see, Mr. Speaker, the great necessity there is for something being done to help this industry. It is an industry which is not only of great value to my district, but it is an industry which is of interest to all of British Columbia, to the North-west, to Manitoba, aye, and to Eastern Canada as well. If I were urging something that was only local in its character, I would not have such a strong case in coming to this House and to the government to ask for assistance. But, Sir, this is an industry which concerns the whole of Canada, and in which all Canada has deep concern.
Now, Sir, this falling off in the production of the mines is not due in any sense to the fact that the mines have petered out. ' The silver lead mines of the Slocan and of the East Kootenay are in a more advanced stage of development to-day than they have been in any period in the history of lead mining in British Columbia. They have ore in great quantity, and the ore is just as valuable as ever it was. It has been suggested by some that the falling off might be attributed to exorbitant freight charges on the railways and exorbitant treatment charges by the smelters, but I can assure the House that such is not the case. The mines are as productive as ever ; the ore is there to be taken out, and the railways and smelters have made cut after cut in their rates in order to try and keep that industry alive. There was a two day's session in the city of Nelson, last fall, where the representatives of the silver lead mining industry met the smelter people and the railway people, and threshed the matter out. The representatives of the silver lend mines in British Columbia satisfied themselves then, that they were receiving fair treat-

ment both from the railway companies and from the smelters. In fact I am told that the rates charged were even better than the rates given to our neighbours across the line. It may be asked :	What then is the
cause of this slump in lead mining in British Columbia. Well it is due to more causes than one. In the first place, a good deal of our lead carries silver with it, and the price of silver and lead in the markets of the world is low. The second reason is, that owing to the conditions that prevail we cannot get any appreciable amount of the Canadian market for the Canadian product of lead. We are thrown into competition with cheap Mexican and Spanish lead which is foisted into Canada through the United States and through Great Britain. Another reason, and a very strong reason is, that during 1900 and prior to that for some years we were shipping our lead ores into the United States first, under the old Wilson tariff of three-quarters of a cent a pound, but afterwards the Dingley tariff raised the rate to one and a half cents a pound against us. When we had the American market for our products, our mines were going ahead, everything was prosperous with ns, and we were able to carry on our works to their fullest capacity. But suddenly what is known as the American Smelting Trust was formed, and so soon as that trust came into existence all the smelters gave notice that at the expiration of the contracts which they then had with the mine owners of British Columbia, they would take no more Canadian ore. Therefore, the American market has been shut off to Canada by the action of that trust. Now when these conditions got to be practically unbearable, when it was seen that unless something was done to relieve the lead miners, that industry would perish ; we in the lead mining district, got together to devise some scheme which we could present to the government for our relief. As the member for the district, I caused notices to be inserted last fall in the papers, asking that a meeting should be called at some stated place to discuss as to the best means of bringing about relief. That notice was heartily responded to and a meeting was called at Sandon which is probably the centre of the lead mining district. That was a very representative meeting and all the lead mines of any importance in British Columbia were represented. The managers, or engineers, or superintendents, as the case may be, met at Sandon, and after carefully discussing the question, action was taken. I may say that the men who attended that meeting were men whose daily avocation is the operating of mines ; men who should be, to my mind, in the best position to judge of what would grant the most relief to that industry in its depression. It was unanimously decided at the Sandon meeting that a delegation should be sent to Ottawa to present the facts to the government, and

to ask them to give us a duty on our lead that would be sufficient to place our miners -not exactly in the position of the American miners, because we felt that we could not get that-but at all events to place them in a position so that they would be able to work their mines to advantage.
What do you think a sufficient duty on lead would be ?
What was asked was practically the Dingley tariff, which is two and one-eighth cents a pound on pig lead, and two and seven-eighth cents a pound, I think on corroded lead.
Would that be adequate V

Yes, that would be adequate, but I have some hesitation in using the word adequate after the explanation of its meaning given by my hon. friend from Brant (Mr. Heyd). As I have said, that was the decision arrived at at that meeting. The Sandon meeting was afterwards followed by a meeting at the city of Nelson where these industries were again represented, and at the meeting in the city of Nelson the resolution of the meeting held in Sandon was practically endorsed. That was followed up, as I said before, by a meeting between the mine owners and those representing the railway and smelting interests in order that the mine owners might be convinced that the railways and smelters were dealing fairly by them both in regard to railway rates and smelting charges. The meeting ended by the mine owners being perfectly satisfled on these points. It was followed by a third and last meeting in the city of Sandon, where again all these interests were represented and the original resolution was re-endorsed. At that meeting certain delegates were appointed to come to Ottawa to interview the government with regard to that resolution ; and I may say that the men who composed that delegation were all practical men, men whose daily avocation was the operating of mines and the treatment of ores, men who understood the A B C of mining, and were capable of presenting the case to the government in a proper light, and who did present that case to the government in a much abler manner than I am presenting it to the House to-night. These delegates were assisted by Mr. Buchanan, who represented the federated Boards of Trade, a gentleman who probably has given more time to this question than any one else. So that our case was very strongly presented to the government, and we hoped that the government, if it could not see its way clear to go to the extent we asked in adjusting the duties, would at all events give us what we all claimed was our right, and what I claim to-night on the floor of this House is the right of our people-to have the tariff on our lead industries so adjusted that it should be placed upon a parity with the other industries of Canada. That, I claim, the people and the lead mining industry of British

Columbia are entitled to. The government have intimated, through the Finance Minister in his budget speech, that they do not see their way to interfere at all at this session of parliament with the tariff respecting lead notwithstanding the great anomaly that exists.
I was pleased to see that the government have asked for power, if certain conditions arose, to impose a duty on steel rails. I think that principle is right. The manufacture of steel rails is a new industry in Canada ; it may become a very important industry ; and when we have the raw material and the means of converting that raw material into the finished article, I believe in the principle of encouraging all new industries of that description. Such, I claim, is our position with regard to lead. When the present tariff was framed, we had no such industry as lead mining in Canada ; therefore, lead was practically put on the free list. Now that we have demonstrated beyond a question the value and importance of the industry and the fact that it can more than supply the demands of Canada, surely we should be placed in a position at least to control our own markets instead of seeing the lead in the different forms in which it is used in Canada come from the cheap Mexican or Spanish article, while our mines of British Columbia are shut down.
Now, I take it that the government, in asking power to place a duty of ?7 a ton on steel rails, have placed themselves on record as willing to assist a new industry under special conditions. There could not be a stronger special case made out than has been made out on behalf of our lead industry. It is an exceptionally special case ; but the lion. Minister of Finance stated, as the reason why he had practically differentiated between the steel rail industry and the lead industry, that to have afforded the relief asked for the lead industry would have necessitated interfering with a great many other items in the tariff. That may be true :	but let us see if that is a good
reason. Having once placed themselves on record as adopting the principle of assisting a new industry under special circumstances, and having applied it to a certain case, under special circumstances, I contend that they should apply the same principle to the second case of special circumstances. The fact that the application of the principle to the second case may involve a little more trouble in working it out, does not, to my mind, affect the question. The point is. is the principle established ? If it is, they should apply it in all similar cases, even if one case involves a little more difficulty than another.
In a country such as Canada is-a growing country, a country of great possibilities, a country where the conditions are changing with wonderful rapidity from year to year, and even in shorter periods-I think no government should lay down any hard and fast j policy that must govern everything. I think
there should be elasticity in the policy of every government. I think special circumstances should be dealt with specially, apart from any fixed principle or policy. If there is justice in the demand, justice should be done. It is all very well for an old country like England to adopt hard and fast rules of policy. It is different in Canada, where conditions are not settled, but where they are constantly changing, and those conditions should be met by any government in power, be it Liberal or Conservative.
Taking into consideration the sums of money which have been invested in that industry in that country, considering the importance of that Industry, not alone to British Columbia but to the North-west Territories as well, it seems to me to call for some energetic action on the part of the government. There is no other industry, not even the mining of other precious metals which so effects the entire province as does the industry cf silver lead mining. Not only does the whole province feel the evil effects of the condition now prevailing, but those evil effects are also visited on the North-west Territories. No doubt the territories are prosperous at present, and I hope that they will long continue so. There is a large immigration pouring into them, but we must not lose sight of the fact that, right at their threshold in the province of British Columbia do they find their natural market for their agricultural products. That province furnishes a very good market for the products of the farm and the ranch. We require large quantities of butter, cheese, hay, oats, cattle, hogs and various other products of the farm and the ranch, and these we get from the North-west Territories. Thus the territories find in our province a remunerative market, and they are backing us up in our application. We have received endorsation from numerous boards of trade throughout the territories and also from the boards of trade of the city of Winnipeg and other places in the province of Manitoba. Aye, Mr. Speaker, we have even received the support of the boards of trade in many parts of Ontario. So that we are not standing alone. _ We alone are not affected, but other provinces share in our loss, and that surely ought to appeal to the favourable consideration of this government. Seven years ago I found this silver mining district, which, a very few years before, had been a solitary wild, a business centre and hum of industry. The bustle of life and business was evident everywhere. Prospectors, miners, investors, business men were pouring in from all quarters, putting their capital into the country, either in mining or business venture. Mining camps, villages, towns and ambitious cities were springing up with incredible rapidity. Times were good, everybody was prospering, and the people naturally looked to a continuance of this condition. All the indications pointed to that district as being a profitable one for the investment of cap:-

tal, and the people invested largely. Bat if the present conditions o? affairs is to continue, if there is to be no help for us, [DOT]what does it mean ? It means ruin to every one of those business men -who invested their money there, and there are numerous towns in that silver lead district in which vast sums have been invested. The mine owners may close down their mines and leave the country. But the merchant, the man who has his money invested in business, cannot do that. There are bills to meet, and there are vast sums of money sunk in stores and buildings, which, if abandoned, will be irredeemably lost. It was suggested, however, by the hon. Minister of Finance-and that I confess is a ray of hope to me-that there would be some readjustment with regard to bounty and that a bounty would take the place of a duty. Well, I was pleased to hear the hon. minister say so, and I hope that the bounty will be a liberal one. An adequate bounty would tide us over our difficulties for a time until the government could see its way clear to give us at least a fair, proportionate and reasonable adjustment of duties, so that our lead products, at all events, would be on the same basis as other products of Canada.
Hear, hear.
If the government decides to grant us a bonus, I wish; to point out that if it is to be of any practical value, it will have to be an adequate one.
Hear, hear.
A sufficient bonus, a liberal bonus.
Hear, hear.

There are two things we should not lose sight of in this connection. I wish you, Sir, to bear in mind that the province of British Columbia contributes to the Dominion treasury more per capita than any other province and three times as much per capita as the average of the other provinces. I would also point out that it contributes in revenue to the coffers of this Dominion some $2,000,000 per annum more than is expended in that province. I do not mention this to say that it should be the policy of the government to expend in any one province all the money paid into its treasury by that province. ' But I merely wish to show that in asking for a large bonus, the province of British Columbia is not drawing from the revenue or resources of any other province of the Dominion. Some two years ago there was an Act Placed on the statutes providing for the payment of a bounty for refining lead. The purpose of this was to have our home product refined at home, that it might not be sent abroad to San Francisco or some other point, and freight charges and smelting charges paid upon it. That bounty ran for five years, and was $5 per ton for the Mr. GALLIHER.
first year, $4 per ton for the second year, $3 per ton for the third year, $2 per ton for the fourth year, and $1 per ton for the fifth year, but in no year might the bounty exceed $100,000. In order to gain the whole bounty the first year, it would have been necessary that 20,000 tons of lead should be mined in Canada. That bounty, so far, has cost very little to the country from the fact that the establishment of refineries cost considerable money. The only parties who took advantage of it was the Canadian Pacific Refining Company at Trail, a town near the silver lead mining district. They have expended some $40,000 or $50,000 in a plant, and in an experiment in refining lead which was then tried for the first time outside a laboratory. The system experimented with has been demonstrated to be successful. It is known as the electrolytic system. The plant at the present time is capable only of turning out some 8,000 or 10,000 tons per annum. When the mining conditions again become normal in British Columbia, lhat plant will have to be largely increased. In view of the fact that the company have shown enterprise and have introduced this new system which is successful, and is in furtherance of science, and in view of the fact that; probably only about $10,000 of the bonus for the year ending 30th June, has been earned, I would ask that the time be extended for a year, within which they may earn bounty at the rate of $5 per ton. Now, this bounty that already exists and the bounty that we propose asking must be treated separately. It will not answer the purpose of the producer of lead for us merely to have a modification in some way of the existing bounty paid to the refiner. What we will ask for, what we shall require in order that this industry may be stimulated by way of bounty, will be a bounty payable directly to the producer of the lead. Here is the man to whom, we claim, if we are to receive assistance, by way of a bounty, that bounty must be paid. Taking the average price of lead for the last twenty years, and taking our settlement at the London prices, it brings to the producer about $1.75 per hundred weight. By the closest and most careful figuring, the gentlemen who have had the matter in hand have decided that it is impossible for the mine owners in that district, outside of a very few whose quota would be small, to operate their mines successfully for less than a return of $2.50 per hundred weight for their lead. So, allowing for the price of $1.75, the bonus should be such as would give to the producer the difference between $1.75 and $2.50, or 75 cents per hundred weight, or $15 per ton. That is the bonus that will be asked. I may say that, since the speech of the Finance Minister was published throughout the country, I have received numerous telegrams, and resolutions from boards of trade both in the territories and throughout the entire province of Brit-

ish Columbia, urging upon me that I should ask the government to reconsider the question of the adjustment of duties, so far as lead is concerned. I am only a young parliamentarian, and I do not know whether this can be done or not. I see no reason why not. At all events, X am going to ask that it be done, that the Minister of Finance reconsider the question in regard to the readjustment of the duties and the bonus to be given us. As to duties, I will only ask them to touch one item, this item of corroded lead. We are assured by two separate concerns that, if a duty of 30 per cent is put on corroded lead, they are prepared to establish corroded works in the east here. If they do so-and they are responsible people-it means the establishment of a new industry in Canada, the expenditure of money in Canada, and the employment of labour in Canada ; and it means the securing the white or corroded lead market for the Canadian producer of lead. It is something, I think, worthy of consideration. And if it is possible or in accordance with the rules to reconsider that and bring it down by way of what we may term a supplementary budget, I would ask the Finance Minister and the government to do so. We in that country are placed in a position where, if adequate relief is not afforded us, either in one way or another, we can see the destruction of those erstwhile live businesslike towns that have sprung up in that country. We do not want that to occur. The people of my district are extremely excited over the matter as it is now ; and I urge in all earnestness upon the government and, if the government bring in any measure of relief I will urge in all earnestness upon the members of the House, to give this matter all due consideration. I hope I have made it clear enough that we are in dire need of assistance in one way or the other in regard to that great industry. We do not wish to see an industry of such magnitude perish ; we do not wish to see our country supplied with the products of other countries while we have within our own border an industry of this kind more than capable of supplying our wants. I care not how the government reach it, so long as they reach it.
Now I have done with the lead question, and before closing I wish to call the aten-tion of the government to another matter. We have in my district, in what is known as the Kelowna valley, along the shores of Ijake Okanagan, in Yale county, one of the finest tobacco growing districts in Canada, ft has been demonstrated that we have in that district 10,000 acres of tobacco land, capable of producing 8,000,000 pounds of tobacco leaf, an article equal in every respect to the best tobacco grown in the United States and imported by Canada, in respect of that matter, I am asking the government to do two things. First, repeal an Order in Council which was passed in June,
1901, allowing factories importing foreign leaf into Canada a rebate of ten cents per pound on foreign leaf cuttings exported from Canada. The meaning of that is this : When factories using foreign leaf import quantities of the same into Canada there is a duty payable thereon, and when they export from Canada the cuttings of this foreign leaf they receive from the government a rebate of ten cents per pound. Now that is all very well if you want to encourage the importation of foreign tobacco, or if you want to discriminate against Canadian grown tobacco*. But when we have demonstrated that we grow in that Kelowna valley tobacco equai to the best imported from the United States, and that that industry is not expanding simply because we cannot sell a pound of our tobacco to those factories that import the foreign tobacco, then something should be done ; and we call for the repeal of that Order in Council, that iniquitous order, which discriminates against our own product and hampers our own industries. , They will not buy from us, because if they do they will not get a rebate on the cuttings. Why sliould we close the door of these factories to the producer of the home grown article ? This question affects the county of Kent, the county of Essex, and all other counties in Canada that grow tobacco. Our tobacco leaf has been pronounced by experts, both from the United States and from Toronto and Montreal, in fact all the leading cities of Canada where tobacco is used, equal to the best grade of American tobacco. Last year I think something like 60,000 pounds only was grown In our district; between 60,000 pounds and 8,000,000 pounds there is, as you will see, a good margin to work on. I, therefore, ask that this Order in Council of 1901 be repealed, so that we may be in a position to sell to all the factories in Canada. I will read an extract from a letter of one of the largest tobacco growers in the Kelowna valley :
Samples of the tobacco I now have ill stock have been shown to all the largest manufacturers in Montreal, London, Toronto, &c., and declared by them to be equal to anything grown in the United States, but in face of this Order in Council I am unable to sell to any foreign leaf factory. To one firm, an actual sale of 6,000 pounds at excellent prices was made, provided it could be taken into the factory free of duty. They ascertained that this could be done, but if they took it in, the rebate on their cuttings would be lost. As their annual rebate amounted to more than the value of the tobacco, the deal of course fell through. I have tried factory after factory with the same result. In no case has any exception been taken to the quality of the leaf, its exclusion is due solely to this Order in Council, and as long as it is in force we shall practically be debarred from selling to foreign factories.
Now, I say there is something that can be remedied without interfering with the tariff, and the remedy should be applied at once.

It is an injustice to our tobacco growers in Canada, it is a discrimination against our tobacco growers in Canada, it is an encouragement of tlie importation of tlie foreign product, when we can produce tlie leaf of equal quality in our own country.
The next thing I want to ask is that only one license stamp be used, allowing all manufacturers to use the domestic and foreign leaf in any proportion they please. I understand by a ruling of the Department of Inland Revenue that the domestic leaf is allowed into factories free of duty. So far so good. But I would ask that this distinguishing stamp be taken off. Originally there were two licenses issued, one for factories in which nothing but foreign leaf was used In the manufacture of cigars. That particular license was accompanied by a gray stamp. A gray inland revenue stamp was the distinguishing mark, showing that that tobacco had been imported from some foreign country and was manufactured solely from imported leaf. The other license was what was known as a domestic license for domestic factories, in which cigars were manufactured entirely from domestic leaf, the distinguished stamp being green. But as Canadian growers gained experience, after they had brought their tobacco leaf up to a high standard, a third license was issued for combination factories, which allowed the manufacturer to make cigars partly from the domestic and partly from the imported tobacco, so long as not less than 25 per cent of the one was used in it. This amount of 25 per cent was afterwards reduced, and is now ten per cent of either domestic or imported, the distinguishing stamp being red. Now what is the object ? We have in Canada a tobacco leaf equal to any that can be imported from the United States. What is the necessity of having a different coloured stamp on our cigar boxes ? Some claim that the stamp merely marks it as Canadian tobacco, or as combination tobacco, or as all imported tobacco. I do not think one smoker in a hundred knows anything about that. He knows what brand of cigars he likes, he buys them and he smokes them ; and I claim that the use of this distinguishing mark is practically black-eying our own products, and encouraging the public to buy an article imported from foreign countries.
Now, if the object is to protect the smoker, as it more nearly affects him, do these distinguishing marks in any way protect the smoker ? We all know that there are as many grades of imported cigars as there are of domestic cigars. They range in price all the way from probably $20 or $30 per thousand to $120 per thousand. There are all these different grades and they all bear the same stamp. Is there any protection in it for the smoker ? No. You buy a certain brand of cigar and smoke it and if you do not like it you try another brand. The smoker is perfectly capable of taking Mr. GALLIHER.
care of himself and if the using of these different stamps has the effect of stamping the Canadian product as inferior in any way to the imported product, then, these stamps should be removed and we should have a uniform stamp placed on all cigars manufactured in Canada. Now, I discussed this matter with the lion. Minister of Inland Revenue (Hon. Mr. Bernier) and he seemed to anticipate that there would be some difficulty in bringing this about; there may be; still I leave the matter to the consideration of the government. I think, myself, and I think any man who will reason it out will come to the same conclusion, that we should not either stamp our goods or exclude the sale of our goods in any factory in Canada to the betterment: of the American product and the encouragement and building up of the industry in the United States or any other country.
Come over;, we will take you.
I am not travelling.
You might as well.

Let us consider for a moment the effect which this system has. Hon. gentlemen know how great the industry is in the United States. I do not know much about the conditions in Essex, or Kent, or in other counties in the east where tobacco is grown, but I do know what we are capable of producing in the west. I know the area that we have that is available for the growing of tobacco and I know that so soon as the conditions are made such that the people have a free hand and can act freely that industry will be started and will be prosecuted to the fullest extent. I, therefore, Mr. Speaker, leave these two matters to the consideration of the government. The more vital one is certainly that of the lead ore mining industry. The other, I consider, also, of great importance and I hope that if the government decide not to in any way interfere in regard to the adjustment of the tariff on lead at the present session they will not allow another session to go by without giving us the relief that we ask for.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the hon. member for Yale and Cariboo (Mr. Galliher), who has just taken his seat, is entitled to the fullest sympathy' of both sides of the House. He has made, certainly, a very strong appeal on behalf of British Columbia industries. He has pointed; out to the government the mistakes they have made in dealing with that province, and so far as I am concerned, I must say that I deeply sympathize with him in the position in which he finds himself placed. When the hon. gentleman began his address, or very shortly afterwards, I noticed that not a single Minister of the Crown was to be found in the Chamber.
I wap here.
Not so. Tlie hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) is very rarely absent indeed.
It is not very important, but I may say that I was not out of the Chamber at any moment when the hon. gentleman (Mr. Galliher) was addressing the House.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. Mr. Fielding).

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. minister was in the gallery.

I know quite well where the hon. minister was; he was concealed behind a post in the upper gallery feeling quite sure that the bullets of lead with which he knew the hon. member for Yale and Cariboo was loaded would not hit him because the pillar was between him and the hon. gentleman.
He was in good company.

The hon. member for Yale and Cariboo tells the House that the budget speech was very nice, that it was very rosy, and that he was delighted with it. No doubt, when he heard of the enormous surpluses that we had during the past year and in prospect for the current year he fully expected that British Columbia would receive some kind of fair treatment, but, io and behold, he said that at the end of that speech there was a bitter pill for British Columbia. Well, Sir, that hon. gentleman does not seem to be alone in finding bitter pills in the budget speech of the hon. Minister of Finance. We find yesterday the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes) bewailed the fact that the salt industry in his town had received no consideration from the government. He was a protectionist ou salt but possibly on nothing else. I do not like to characterize the hon. gentleman as a parish politician, but I have not very much regard for those protectionists who are simply protectionists in a local way. I believe that we should have the same policy for the whole country and for all the industries in the country. If the hon. gentleman was right in his contention that the salt industry should receive the paternal care of the government, why would lie refuse that paternal care to other industries which were all of just equal importance and perhaps of very much greater importance ? The hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell) stands along with the hon. member for Yale in his constituency. Thousands of people are engaged in the production of vegetables for the market in Toronto and elsewhere. That hon. gentleman, when last returned to this House, I believe, secured his election by his pledge to secure for those people additional protection for that important industry. Yet, we find him here, to use an expression of his own, like a bump on a log, saying nothing at all and leaving
his constituents to suffer whilst the government takes no action in regard to the matter. The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) has become a protectionist for the cream separator manufacturers. Where is he going to be when the resolution moved by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) is voted upon ? is he1 going to declare that the cream separator manufacturers of Guelph are not entitled to adequate protection. I question very much if he would not prefer being outside of the Chamber when the vote is taken, even if he should only be in tlie gallery. Then we had the member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd) appealing on behalf of the town of Brantford and its industries. Binder twine lias given him a large amount of trouble, and the government thinks they have fairly met him, with the slight aid of riiree-eiglits of one cent a pound, whilst if our Brantford factory would send a pound of twine to the United States they would be met with a duty of two cents a pound. Then we had the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Galliher) appealing on behalf of the lead industry and the tobacco industry in his section of the country, for some material assistance. If I remember aright, we bad the member for Alberta (Mr. Davis) anxious that a duty should be placed upon borses or at any rate that an increased valuation should be put on horses so that the duty as it at present exists could be made effective in protecting the horse breeders of the west. But I was rather amazed at the member for Yale (Mr. Galliher). 1 was amazed at how well he enjoyed the bitter pill that was given him by the government. He said he had hopes. Well, there is an old saying about living in hope and dying in despair, and I am afraid that will be the lot of the member for Yale. It is no new thing to hear this appeal from British Columbia for assistance to the mining industry, but year after year goes on and the government declares that there is no necessity for doing anything for that province, because they know perfectly well that the member for Yale and others of his kidney will give them their support through thick and thin.
I was much pleased indeed at the reference which the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) made in his budget speech to the postal revenue of this country, and there was probably a good reason why the Minister of Finance should refer to it. His duty is to give a fair statement of the revenues and expenditures and I was pleased at his reference to that service because to a certain extent it corrected the statement that had gone abroad in the country-not with the intention of misleading any one I must suppose-that the Post Office Department had been so well administered that it actually showed a surplus of revenue over expenditure. The friends of the government throughout the country spoke of this with
\

great delight and great pleasure. It was the one department that showed anything like economy, and they held it up to the people as an evidence on the part of the government of a desire to fulfil their pledges as to economy. Be that as it may I fail to see why continued reference should be made to it in a budget debate. My opinion, and I think that opinion is well founded because I have carefully investigated the matter ; my opinion is that any decrease in the deficit of the Post Office Department has been brought about simply by starving the service. Men are to-day performing duties under the Postmaster General at starvation wages. It is unfair in a country like this that men should be called on to discharge such duties for the miserable pittance they receive. I refer more especially to the country postmasters, and to the mail carriers as well who have arduous duties to perform and who as a rule are not sufficiently paid. I have said, and I am prepared to back up my statement with substantial proof, that this starvation of the service alone is responsible for the alleged saving in the Post Office Department. On June 30, 1891, there were 8,061 post offices in operation in Cau-ada, and in 1896 when the Conservative government left power there were 9,103 or an increase in the five years of 1,042 post offices, or an average yearly increase of 208. Let us compare this with the conditions under the present government. On the 30th of June, 1902, there were 9,958 post offices in Canada or an increase of only 855 over the number in 1896, as against an increase in the last live years of Conservative rule of 1,042. There was an average increase during the regime of the Liberal government of only 142 per year compared with 208 per year during the last five years of the Conservative government. We have heard of the new areas that have been opened up recently to settlement in the North-west and in New Ontario, and during these past five or six years there must have been much more numerous demands for increased postal facilities than there were during the previous five years, but notwithstanding that, we find that the people of Canada are left without postal conveniencies simply in order that one member of the administration may be able to say that he had administered his department with only a small loss. Had the same rate of increased accommodation been given to the people of Canada during the last six years that had been given during the last five years of the Conservative regime, we would have today 400 more post offices opened in the Dominion of Canada than we have at present. Now, Sir, if we have large surpluses; if we have money to burn, how could we spend it better than in providing comforts, conveniencies and accommodation for our people, and I know of no way in which public money can be spent to better advantage Mr. HENDERSON.
than in giving the people of the country better post office facilities.
With reference to the financial statement of the Minister of Finance I intend to have very little to say. I congratulate hon. members who have preceded me, during the latter part of the debate especially, on the new policy of short speeches in this House, and I intend to-night not to break that, which I regard as a very wholesome rule.
Hear, hear.

bounty on the one-tenth part of the sugar consumed in this country would be very small compared with the tax we are paying on the 400,000,000 pounds which we are consuming at present. I would give the people cheap sugar, but X would assist by a bounty the farming community in the districts where beet sugar may be produced; the growing of which has ceased to be profitable in the province of Ontario. Our farmers will tell you that. In our province we do not eat bread made from the flour ground from our own wheat, but largely from the flour we import from Manitoba. Consequently the growing of wheat in Ontario is not as profitable as it was. The cattle industry is also showing signs of failure, and practically our Ontario farmers have now only two industries on which they can rely-dairying and hog raising ; and they are attempting to supplement these industries by the introduction of a new one, that of producing their own sugar. I, therefore, hope that the government will see its way clear to give an adequate bounty in order that this new industry may be assisted and become a success in the province of Ontario, and the other provinces where it may be started.
We have heard a great deal in this debate about the reduction of taxation, but I must confess that, in my examination of the tariff and its results, as shown by the Trade and Navigation Returns, I am at a loss to find where this boasted reduction in taxation comes in. I find that the average rate of taxation is just about what it was under the Conservative regime. I do not consider that there is one-hundredth part of a cent difference to-day between the average rate of taxation in the first five years of Liberal rule and the last five years of Conservative rule. Any one who will take the trouble to investigate and make a fair comparison will find such to be the case, and that is just what the lion. Minister of Finance intended. He told us three years ago that he never intended to reduce taxation. Let me quote his own words :
It was of the utmost importance that we should maintain a strong financial position and in view of the uncertainties as to the amount of revenue that might be produced by this lower rate of taxation it became necessary that we should take some steps to make good any possible loss that might result. It was thought that it might fairly be met by providing for the raising of some additional taxation in order to balance, or make good, the loss occasioned by
the reduction of duties....It was necessary
to have an increased revenue in certain directions when we were to lose revenue in other directions.
That policy the hon. gentleman carried out. He simply has taken off something here and put something on there, but unfortunately he has upset the trade of the country by the unfair way in which he has balanced up the revenue. For example he taxes the workingman heavily on sugar.
