The hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Schell) I thought, went somewhat out of his way this afternoon to show what the government has done for the farmers. I say he went somewhat out of his way, because the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes) told us that it was absolutely impossible for the government to protect the farmers. So here is a queer difference between these two gentlemen, one holding strongly to the opinion that the farmer cannot be protected, the other holding as strongly to the opinion that the government had been protecting the farmer. I turned up the report of the Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher) for 1897, the first year of the Liberal government. The report was written and printed very shortly after hon. gentlemen opposite came into power. I turned to this report in order to find out for myself practically who it was that established cold storage in this country. I think it is only fair that X should read an extract from that report, for I am under the impression that many people in this country are a little mistaken on this question. This report gives what the Minister of Agriculture had to say in 1S97, before he became contaminated with these extraordinary ideas which seem to prevail on the other side. This is when he came in fresh from the farm. For you know, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Agriculture is a farmer, a practical farmer, an innocent youth, who, at this time was just off the farm and did not know how to misrepresent a thing, but told the facts as he found them. An hon. gentleman beside me remarks that he was green. I did not think he was. I think he was all right. He came from the farm and showed the honesty of a farmer. It is somewhat remarkable, after all the boasting I have heard of the Minister of Agriculture being a farmer that, a very short time ago, he called to his assistance, as chief executive officer of his department, a lawyer. Has the hon. gentleman lost confidence in himself ? Has he lost confidence in the ability of a farmer to administer that department ? Has the department given him a great deal of trouble ? Or what is the difficulty that has caused him to call in a lawyer in this way ? I have here what he said in his innocent youthful days when he was fresh from the farm and could not tell anything but the truth.
A cold storage service for the safe carriage of butter was begun in 1895.
Who were in power in 1895 ? Why the Conservatives.
Arrangements were made whereby refrigerator cars for carrying butter were run during the summer on the main lines of railways leading into Montreal. These cars were used to pick up small lots of butter as offered at the different railway stations. Shippers by these 664
cars were allowed to ship butter at the usual * less than car-load rates,' without any charge for icing or special service. As far as space permitted, merchants were allowed to use these cars for the shipment of dairy and creamery butter between points at which the cars touched. During 1895 cars were run for at least part of the season on the Grand Trunk and Canadian Pacific railways.
Arrangements were also made for the chilling of fresh-made creamery butter at the warehouses of the Montreal Cold Storage and Freezing Company, Montreal.
Arrangements were made for the fitting up of insulated and refrigerator chambers on steamships from Montreal to Avonmouth, Liverpool and Glasgow. The chambers were constructed to thoroughly insulate

Observe the word ' thoroughly ' and contrast it with what the hon. gentleman said
-their contents, and thus prevent them from being heated during the voyage by any rise of temperature outside the chamber. Galvanized iron cylinders were filled with ice to cool the interior of the chamber and the outside of the packages of the butter, in so far as they were heated during the cartage from the cold storage warehouses to the steamships.
And I find that, during the shipping season of 1894 there were exported from the port of Montreal 32,055 packages of butter. In 1895 the shipments were 69,664 packages and in 1896, 157,321 packages. And yet we listened this afternoon for upwards of half an hour to the hon. member for Glengarry trying to convince this House that the present government had established the cold storage system. I wonder that if, even today, after seven years, when the cold storage system is much better understood than in 1895, they have a very much better system than was established by the former government I think that Dr. Montague, the former Minister of Agriculture is entitled to the credit of establishing that boon to the people of this country-cold storage. It is like everything else that has been inaugurated for the benefit of the farmers-it emanated from the Conservative party. Now, the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes) is willing that the farmers should pay an increased price for salt in order to benefit the town of Clinton where he chances to reside, because he wants adequate protection on salt. But I do not know whether it is for the manufacturer he wants it or for the farmer. It is the farmer who must pay the increased price if there is an increase; but, he would not need to pay it, because he could still buy his Canadian salt. And I have no doubt that he could get that salt just as cheaply if the duty were doubled. In fact, I believe that if the duty were doubled the Canadian farmer would buy his salt cheaper. In that respect, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Holmes) is a sound protectionist, he has the right principle; but he does not want to apply it to anything but salt. If he would apply it to woollen goods and cotton goods

and others, we would welcome him on this side, and would be glad to see him advocate so sound a policy for this country with that ability which does him credit. We are told by some bon. gentlemen opposite that the farmers cannot be protected. My opinion is that the farmers are protected. Some may have different ideas of protection from my own. But in my opinion to protect an industry does not mean to put it in a position to demand a higher price. To protect the farmer or to protect the woollen or cotton manufacturers is to give the market of this country to the farmer or to the manufacturer. You protect the farmers of this country when you give them the market of the country. For instance, we put a duty of thirty-five per cent on mutton, and that keeps American mutton out. Last year only $2,879 worth of mutton and lamb came into this country. The whole market of Canada with this exception was kept for the farmers of this country. That was 'adequate protection,' if hon. gentlemen opposite want to know what adequate protection is. Of fresh meats other than lamb and mutton we imported $38,198 worth. On this article there is a duty of three cents a pound.
Well, I think that three cents a pound is fairly adequate protection on an article that costs about six cents a pound. It is very good protection, and that is the protection that we believe in giving the farmers of this country. Not that we say for one moment that we are going to help the farmer to get two prices for his article, that is not the meaning of it; but we say we will put a Chinese wall right round this country, and we will not allow these Americans to come in here and monopolize the markets of this country when they do not contribute anything towards the expenses of this country. The Canadian farmer is entitled to this market, and we put that duty on to enable him to get this market, and to retain it. Fork, two cents a pound. I do not think that is adequate protection, because there were $561,414 worth of pork brought in. I believe the minister will be wise if he increases that duty to three cents and gives the Canadian farmers adequate protection. Pickled beef or barrelled beef, $77,554 worth imported. The farmers are fairly well protected on that article. The market is fairly well held by the farmers of this country. Bacon and hams, only two cents a pound. I do not think the protection is adequate. If it were made three cents we might exclude a very large amount of this $635,831 worth of bacon and ham that came in, and which we could produce in this country just as good, and, I believe a great deal better than that we get from the other side. Butter, $160,459. The farmer of this country is protected to the extent of four cents a pound. That is the duty put on to prevent tlie American farmer from coming into this country, and it is fairly successful in giving

the farmers of this country the market of Canada. Of cheese, $31,368 worth came in under a protection of three cents. If three cents a pound is not sufficient, I would say add more. It will not increase the price of cheese in this country, because what signifies $31,368 worth compared with all the cheese that is consumed in Canada and all that is exported out of the country. That three cents a pound on cheese has no effect whatever on the price of cheese to the consumer. It does not enhance it to the thousandth part of a cent, but it does give the farmer in this country all the market we have for cheese, and that is what the farmer has a right to ask. Flour, $144,714 worth at 60 cents a barrel. I regret that the present government when they came into power to revise the tariff, interfered with the duty on flour. Formerly it was 75 cents a barrel, and they reduced it to 60 cents, and it remains at that figure still. Wheat, formerly 15 cents, reduced to 12 cents, and yet $S9,470 worth of wheat came into this country. What, bring American wheat into this country ? Cannot Ontario and the great North-west furnish all the wheat that is necessary to feed the people of Canada ? Why should we even admit this small amount of $89,407 worth. I say the duty should be high enough to give the entire market to the people of this country. Oats, $67,223 worth came in under a protection of 10 cents a bushel, a fairly good protection. Pease, 10 cents a bushel, $15,119 worth came in.
Now, going over the list. I take it that the farmers of this country are fairly well protected so far as holding the market of Canada is concerned, and that is one of the objects of agricultural protection. No man ever dreamed that you were going to give the farmers $2 a bushel for his wheat, no man ever dreamed that you were going to give him 50 cents a bushel more than it is worth. No such idea ever prevailed. But it has occurred in this country, and it may occur again, when farmers do receive more than a normal price for wheat. I remember in 1895, in the month of June, when there was a short crop of wheat in this country, that wheat sold in the city of Toronto for 20 cents a bushel more than it sold for in the city of Liverpool. The advantage that a farmer would get in price is only when a short crop occurs, but as long as there is an abundant supply-which we always hope there will be in Canada-no farmer will expect to get an increased price by slightly raising the protection. But he does get the market. Let me give an illustration how he controls the market. In Manitoba we have enormous grist mills, I think there is one mill in Winnipeg turning out about 3,500 barrels a day. In Minneapolis they have an enormous grist-mill grinding the same quantity of wheat. No. 1 hard. The flour from Minneapolis is shipped to the seaboard, possibly it goes to Boston. The flour from

Winnipeg is also sent to the seaboard, and is possibly exported by way of Boston. Suppose a vessel goes down from Halifax loaded with fish and wants a return cargo. The owner goes to the flour dealer and he says : How do you sell flour, or what flour have you got ? He says : I have American flour from Minneapolis, and I have Canadian flour from Winnipeg, both made from No. 1 hard wheat, which will you have ? Well, says the shipper, I will take Canadian. Why does he take Canadian ? Because he knows too well that when he returns to Halifax the Canadian flour, having been shipped through in bond, comes in free of duty, but if he took American flour he would have to pay GO cents a barrel to the revenues of the Dominion of Canada before he could get a market for that flour. The duty of GO cents gives the Canadian farmer the benefit of that market, the benefit of the markets of the maritime provinces and the province of Quebec. It does the same thing in Ontario, because as I told you, in Ontario we do riot consume now the products of our own farms.
The hon. member for Huron (Mr. Holmes) says : Absolutely it is impossible to protect the farmer. Well, what do the farmers say themselves ? Let us take a look around this House. In 1900 we had a general election, and the tariff was the leading question in the province of Ontario. I am prepared to submit that question to the farmers. My hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) is an example of what the farmers think of the principle of protection. North Middlesex sends a supporter (Mr. Sherritt) of the Conservative party, instead of a supporter of the hon. gentleman opposite. East Lambton sent another Conservative (Mr. Simmons), who, I regret to say, has not been able, through illness, to be in the House for some time. He replaced a Liberal who formerly sat on the other side of the House. My hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Thomson) is a living evidence of what the farmers think about protection. My hon. friend from South Grey (Mr. Richardson) is also an evidence that his constituents favour the same principle. The riding of Lincoln has sent in our friend (Mr. Lancaster), another evidence of what the people of the west think about the principle of protection. South Wentworth (Mr. Smith)-why, you find them all over, the House is filled with them. South Waterloo (Mr. Clare), another evidence. West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) also, he replaces one of the most inveterate Liberals we had in the House, and though he may not perhaps, be just what we would like him to be in the way of protection, I believe that his feelings are with us. But he represents a very critical constituency, and he thinks it is just as well to be fair to all sides. However, I hope that when the vote is taken, his conscience will dictate to him what is right, and I am quite sure he will follow his conscience. East Hastings (Mr. Nortlirup), another evideuce of what the farmers of Ontario think of protection. Stormont, I believe, is another. South Victoria (Mr. Vrooinan) is another. What shall I say of West York (Mr. Campbell) ? Had it not been for the principle of protection, I do not believe that the present representative would be in the House. Here is what the farmers themselves say. They say the farmer can be protected and they are going to support the party that endorses the principle of adequate protection. Well then, how are you going to protect the farmer ? I have been endeavouring to tell you that you protect the farmer by protecting his market. You give him the home market for his commodities. In that way he receives the protection that this parliament can extend to him. So long as we keep the home market for him, we do a great deal. It is our duty as well to find foreign markets for his commodities, but in seeking the foreign market the farmer has to enter into competition with countries, such as Argentina and other wheat producing countries where they have cheap labour, thus placing our famers at a disadvantage. If we can seeure the home market in Canada for 80 per cent of the products of the farms of this country, we are doing a great deal for the farmers. It'is estimated that the entire product of the farms of Canada is worth about $500,000,000. We exported last year of animals and agricultural products. $100,000,000, in round numbers ; therefore, we consumed in Canada $400,000,000 worth of the products of the farms, or 80 per cent were consumed in our own market. Is it not a matter of importance that we should protect that home market that consumes 80 per cent of the products of the farms even if we cannot secure the same character of a market for the other 20 per cent ? I say the true policy is to hedge around this country with adequate protection for the farmers and give them all the benefits that can possibly accrue to them by retaining their own market for this large percentage of their output. The city of Montreal has a population of about 2G7.000 people.

Well, I take the last census. Perhaps it is 300,000 now. If we consume in Canada $400,000,000 worth of the products of this country we consume on an average $70 per head worth of the products of the farms. Seventy dollars worth of the products of the farms is the average consumption of every man, woman and child in this country. I do not mean to say that each man, woman and child eats $70 worth of food, not by any means, but there are many things that are not produced on the farm such as horses and cattle, hay, and such things that are not being consumed. The average consumption in one year or another of every individual is $70. Let us look at the value of the city of Montreal with all its varied industries. I

need not attempt to enumerate them us there are bon. gentlemen who know them better than I do. That market is worth to the farmers of this country on that basis $18,000,000 and the city of Toronto is a good second. What would the farms of this country be worth if these industrial institutions were blotted out or were hampered or hindered in carrying on their operations? It would simply paralyze this country and destroy its value. I was in the city of Winnipeg in the month of October last. I admired that growing city. I believe it is destined to be a great city. I do not know the present population, but, according to the last census, it was some 42,000. I dare say it is now 50,000, or perhaps more.

And I suppose in five or ten years iti will have a population of 100,000. I wonder if the people of that country have any fair estimate of the value of the city of Winnipeg to the province! of Manitoba ? According to the calculation I have made 42,000 people would consume each year $3,000,000 worth of the products of the farms of Manitoba, l'n five or ten years I believe the population of that city will be doubled, and instead of $3,000,000 worth they will consume $6,000,000 worth of the products of the farms of Manitoba, affording an enormous market. What would the farmers of Manitoba do without a city like Winnipeg and without the other towns that are growing up in that country ? They would be compelled to ship out of the country all of their surplus products. They would be compelled to ship out yearly nearly a, half million more of their wheat and enormous quantities of the other products that are consumed there. Is it not better to encourage the growth of industries in a place like Winnipeg and encourage the bringing in of a consuming population which is not a producing population, but which will consume the products of the farms of that great province ? I may say the people of Manitoba are not alive to their best interests if they for one moment would hesitate in supporting a party that would give them adequate protection, and that would give to every industry that might grow up in Winnipeg adequate protection. Why should these people not make their own agricultural implements, why should they not make their own harness, why should they not make their own boots and shoes, why should they not make their own clothes, why should they not make their own furniture ? These are all possibilities and if industries of this kind were instituted there, were supported and were maintained there is no doubt at all that that city would become a very great city and become an enormous market for the products of that province and so enhance the value of every farm within range of that crowded centre. If the people of Manitoba say that Mr. HENDERSON.
they approve of that sort of thing let them send to, this parliament representatives who will support the principle of adequate protection, and in due time the capital will go into that country that will be requisite to establish these industries and to give them that market. We have been asked across the floor of the House to state what was meant by adequate protection. I am surprised, I confess, that hon. gentlemen cannot form an adequate opinion of what it means. I think it is very simple indeed. Now, there is an article made in the city of Guelph which is known as a cream separator. There is a very large number of them sold in this country. That article is admitted absolutely free into this country. The hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes) wants protection on salt. Why should he say protect the salt industry and refuse protection to the cream separator industry ? To my mind the cream separator industry is just as important to be protected as the salt industry, or as the lead industry. There were imported last year $4S7.734 worth of cream separators into Canada. There are only two factories, both of them in Guelph making that article. Let me say that the cream separators^ made in Guelph are equal in every respect as to finish as the foreign made article and taking the same capacity they are ns low in price as the article brought in from the United States, or Germany, or Sweden. They are sold alongside of each other. One man buys one, another man buys another. They simply buy a certain separator because a particular agent sells it. There is no particular choice, but, as a matter of fact, there were last year imported into this country about 10,000 cream separators. Let ns consider what an advantage it would be to the city of Guelph if the trade of Guelph were extended by the additional labour that would be required to bring about the manufacture of these goods. Ten thousand cream separators will require a very considerable amount of labour. The money that would be paid for the construction of these machines would be paid out again to the workmen of the city of Guelph. These workmen in turn would pay it out to the farmers for their beef, butter, eggs, cheese, potatoes and flour and all the piroducts of the farm. The money goes back to the farmer and he buys his cream' separator and pays for it. The money simply keeps circulating; it does not go out of the country and you never see it again, as it would if the farmer bought an American separator, or a German separator, or a Swedish separator. The farmers are alive to this fact and they are beginning to see that their true interests lie in the protection of the industries that brings protection to the farmer. That is one of the ways to protect the farmer. If you want to give the farmer true protection, and all the protection you can give, you will have to surround the industries of this country with

a tariff that will force largely the manufacture of goods in this country, so that the markets of Canada will be increased by the addition of an Industrial population who must of necessity live on the products of the farm, and thus enhance the value of the farms.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hoar.
That argument applies not only to the cream separator, but it applies to the woollen industry, to the cotton industry and to every industi'y in this country as well.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The agricultural implement industry to ?

Yes, the agricultural implement industry as well. The trouble in this country at the present time is that we have too much taxation and too little protection. We simply want the Finance Minister to reverse the order-give us a little more protection and less taxation.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

Many lion, gentle-ment in this House seem to.think that high protection means high taxation. That is a most absurd idea. I do not believe that you will get the Finance Minister to propound that doctrine. X do not think that he would sacrifice his reputation and standing by getting up here and telling us that high protection means, of necessity, high taxation. Why it is the reverse. They tell us that their tariff is a tariff for revenue only. Well, it is not that. It is neither one thing or the other. They have a duty of three cents a pound on fresh meat and very little fresh meat comes into Canada. If they want a tariff for revenue only, let them reduce that duty to one cent a pound, and I will undertake to say that they will get three times more revenue than they get now at three cents a( pound. If their tariff is a tariff for revenue only why do they not put a duty on tea and coffee ? We cannot produce these in Canada. . If they are afraid of protecting or helping the people of the country; if they are alarmed that any industry would be benefited by their fiscal policy, let them raise their revenue on tea and coffee and other articles which we cannot produce, and which would not interfere with any industry, -and that would be a tariff f" revenue only. But that is not their policy. They adopted the old Conservative tariff to the extent that they still give us free coffee and free tea. I have said, that what we want is more protection and less taxation, and that if we had that we would not be troubled with these enormous surpluses which the Minister of Finance scarcely knows what to do with. Adequate protection does not mean higher taxation; it means lower taxation. I go further and I say that adequate protection does not mean higher prices. I know that
there are gentlemen in this House who will not agree with me when I say that adequate protection does not of necessity mean higher prices, but I can tell them that if there was 25 per cent put upon cream separators to-day, the farmers of Ontario would buy them for ,$5 less, and if the minister does not credit it, I will undertake to procure for him a bond from those manufacturers that they will do it. If the minister will give a protection sufficiently reasonable .to protect these men and give them the large market of this country, I will undertake to say that the farmers of Canada will benefit to the extent of from $5 to $10 on every separator they buy. And this is the reason. The manufacturer in Guelph sends out his agent to sell cream separators, but he meets agents from the United States, from Germany, from Sweden, from England, all selling cream separators. The country is flooded with the foreign article., and the agent of the Guelph manufacturer is possibly not able to sell more than one machine a day, whereas if he had the whole market within his reach he could possibly sell three times as many. Therefore the manufacturer's agent could sell three machines for the same expense which it now costs him to sell one. In this way the Canadian manufacturer could afford to sell a machine to the farmer for $5 or $10 less, and the manufacturer would have just as much money in his pocket as he lias now. That is an example and it is an example that will apply in very many things. When I was going out to Manitoba last year a manufacturer in my own town said to me : You can tell the people out there that if I were given adequate protection so as to secure the market in this country along with those who manufacture the same article in Canada, I will undertake to reduce my prices 10 per cent; and he could do it if it were nothing) more than his saving on the cost of his travellers who would sell double the quantity they do now at the same expense. I am not one of those who believe in that bugaboo that high protection means high prices. Of course if you make it exclusive, it is another thing, but that is not adequate protection. We are not asking for exclusive protection; we are not asking that everything be excluded. All that we want is adequate; just enough to accomplish the purpose of giving the markets of this country to the Canadian manufacturers and i Canadian; farmers so that they can make a reasonable living profit. I have said that adequate protection does not mean higher taxation, and does not mean higher prices, i but I tell you honestly that it does mean
>
higher prosperity. If you want evidence ! regarding .that you can get it from the . speech of the hon. member for Huron (Mr. * Holmes) yesterday. He gave us a quotation
>
from a pamphlet which he said came into i his possession, and did not doubt the correct-t ness of it. It was a pamphlet he said that

was sent out by the Canadian Cotton Goods Company, and in the pamphlet I find a paragraph headed ' Canadian goods cheap to the consumer,' and he goes on to say :
There is not the least doubt that the Canadian consumer saves nothing on imported goods.
The hon. member for Huron (Mr. Holmes) quoted that as authority. But he gives this as an illustration, and his illustration is a very good one :
. An illustration of this fact recently came to light. A wholesaler imported a line of fancy shirtings and laid them down at eight cents and a half a yard. He sold them to the retailers at eleven and a half cents, who resold at seventeen cents.
A pretty good profit by the way :
A Canadian firm duplicated the pattern; sold it at- eight cents, the wholesaler sold at ten cents, while the consumer got it at twelve and a half cents, meaning a saving of four and a half cents per yard to the wearer of the shirt.
That is a pretty good showing for Canadian goods. Who says that Canadian goods cannot be produced just its cheap as foreign goods ? The Canadian manufacturer was able to compete with his foreign competitor, he was able to reproduce that article at a price below the imported article which he was able to undersell. But what advantage was there in that ? Suppose he was able to do it, where was he going to sell it ? The importers had flooded the country with that class of goods, everybody had been supplied, and when the Canadian turned out his product, he had no market for it. He might sell it at half a cent less, or even at two cents less, yet lie would not find the demand for it, because the demand had been filled. That is the case with very many commodities. Let us take the case of coloured cottons to show how the Canadian manufacturer is handicapped as against the British. The latter has a market in cold climates and in warm climates. The calico printer makes his plates. In the first year the product of those plates is sold in England ; the next year it finds its way to Canada and the United States ; the third year it goes to Australia, possibly to South America ; the fourth year it is sent to South Africa, and some other distant countries ; and the fifth year it is sold in India and Japan, where the latest fashion is not so much thought of. The English manufacturer can turn out goods from the same plates for five years, and turn them out all the year round, because he has markets in colder climates and in warmer climates in various parts of the world, while the Canadian manufacturer lias a limited market in Canada, and can only produce one impression from the same plates. There is no doubt that he is handicapped to a great extent, and an industry of that kind ought to have the help of the government. We have the evidence of the hon. member for

West Huron that the Canadian manufacturer is able to produce these goods at half a cent less than the importer could buy them for in the old country. But he had not fair treatment; he had not adequate protection. It was immaterial whether he produced them or not. If he did, they simply lay on his hands,	because the market had been monopolized by the larger producer in the old country. If there had been adequate protection to keep the English goods out, the moment the Canadian manufacturer produced his goods, he would have been able to get a fair price for them, and the Canadian consumer would have been able to get his goods at four and one-half cents less than he had to pay for the imported article. You cannot expect men to risk their capital in large industries of that kind, unless they are given to understand beforehand that they are going to have the paternal care and protection of the government to guarantee them a fair return for what they produce. Hon. gentlemen opposite have been telling us all along that these goods would be dearer under protection, and we find that statement refuted.
There is one question which I never could solve in listening to hon. gentlemen opposite. They said : Take down the tariff wall and let us get into the United States, and we shall be able to buy everything cheap. Take down the tariff wall of 20 per cent, and we shall get our agricultural implements from Chicago and other places on the other side of the line a great deal cheaper than we get them now. The strange part of it is the people who talk in that way want to get their goods in the most highly protected country in the world. To get cheap goods, they want to go to the highly protected United States, or to highly protected Germany. If these hon. gentlemen reflected for a moment, would they not see the propriety of joining with us and giving a policy of adequate protection to the manufacturers of Canada, so that we could have cheap goods without going out of Canada ? If high protection in the United States makes cheap goods, high protection in this country will make cheap goods as well. I have demonstrated that high protection does not mean higher prices. I think I can safely make this statement without fear of successful contradiction, that y(e never had cheaper agricultural implements in Canada than we had under the 35 per cent tariff, when the national policy was in full swing. We took 15 per cent off, but there was not a drop of 15 per cent in the price. I do not say that a binder or a mower may not cost more money to-day than it did ten or fifteen years ago ; but it is a very different implement from what it was then. It has various improvements and attachments which were not on it at that time, and it is worth more money. I also say, as a practical business man who has been handling goods for
2097'

many years, that we never had cheaper cottons than we had under the national policy. We never had better or cheaper woollen goods than we had under the national policy. We never had cheaper coal oil than we had under the national policy. What do we pay tor it now ? If you want to buy a barrel of Canadian oil in the part of the country where I live to-day, you have to pay 19J cents a gallon for it, whereas we used to pay 121 cents, a difference of 7J cents, although a cent a gallon has been taken off the duty. Barbed wire was cheaper under the national policy than it is to-day, and I understand it is free.
Labour was cheaper too.

Under the national
policy ?
Certainly ; cheaper than it is to-day ; wages were lower.

And wages will be lower again, perhaps, and wages were lower, before the national policy was inaugurated. The hon. minister will remember the days of the soup kitchens under the Mackenzie government, when the labouring classes were praying for a national policy, and when the government were turned out of power because they would not give it-just what this government will come to if they do not give this country adequate protection. Binder twine is nearly double the price to-day that it was under the national policy. It is no better, I suppose. Labour is dearer. How much labour does it take to make a pound of twine ? Seven and a half cents of labour to make one pound of twine ? Great heavens ! It is a big industry. Is it the labour that makes the difference ? Why, I understand that it is made in the penitentiary, where the labour does not cost anything; and yet the price is away up. It cannot be the labour, Mr. Minister; you must be mistaken. I will take a common article now; we will come down just to what any gentleman can understand. Take a common article like sewing thread. Under the national policy, in 1895, a farmer's wife got two spools for five cents, each spool containing 200 yards of the thread. But now she has to pay five cents for one spool. I suppose it is the difference in labour which is the cause. I believe it is the difference in duty. The government destroyed the protective principle applied to the thread industry, and the manufacturers were compelled to join the English combine, which they did and the prices went up. Then take sugar. Why, I remember when we used to shovel out 30 pounds of sugar for a dollar under the old national policy. No doubt the labour again is at fault. Why, I was almost going to say that I was grateful to the government, as a business man, for having made the change, because the labour we had to hire to
weigh it out [DOT] made the business almost unprofitable. I regret very much that my hon. friend, the Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) has gone out. I was going to submit to him a proposition. No doubt, when he gets up to address the House on this question, lie will repeat the old story that high protection means high prices and that the more duty you put on, the more you will enhance prices. The hon. gentleman himself is engaged in a legitimate business, the manufacture of biscuits-a commodity which is practically a spot cash article and for which there is a very large demand throughout the country. There is a duty of twenty-five per cent on common biscuits, not sweetened, and twenty-seven and a half per cent on biscuits sweetened. The hon. gentleman is not responsible for putting that duty on biscuits, for that is just the tariff we left him. We considered that that industry was entitled to that amount of protection. We considered that an adequate protection and the hon. gentleman has never thought fit to change it. I believe that if he thought for one moment that the object of that tariff was to enable him to raise the prices and extort more money out of the pockets of the consumer, he would reduce it. The fact that he has not done so is proof that he believes these duties are perfectly legitimate. If he believed that they were too high, if he believed that they enabled either his firm or any other to extort undue prices for a spot cash article, which enters into the consumption of every family in the country, I am convinced that, as an honest man- which I believe he is-he would reduce that duty. And if he does not do so it is no doubt because he considers it a fair protection, which gives him and the others in that line the market of Canada. That is what these duties are for, and not to enable him or any other manufacturers of biscuits to get extortionate prices. That was not the intention of the Conservative party which imposed the tariff. But what we wanted was to give our Canadian market to our Canadian manufacturers as much as possible. That they have got. I find that we only imported $14,496 worth of sweetened biscuits.
Where from ?
That was the entire importation of sweetened biscuits.
Where from ?
One half came from England.
Under the preferential rate ?
Certainly.
Then one-third was taken off the duty ?
Then the Minister of Customs did reduce the duty. A moment ago you said lie did not.
Does the hon. gentleman not think that water will find its own level.

Yes, and 1 think that the hon. gentleman has struck his level. Ret me tell the hon. gentleman how many of those common biscuits came from the old country, and no doubt he will argue that because we imported $2,189 worth of biscuits from England, that importation reduced the price of the $1,000,000 manufactured in this country. I intended making a short speech, and if I have trespassed more than I intended on the time of the House, at any rate I have introduced a new feature into the debate. I have endeavoured to go along the line of adequate protection and show this House and country the advantages of a system of adequate protection and dissipate the absurd idea that because you protect an industry you of necessity enhance prices, and That high protection means high prices or high taxation. It does not mean either, but what it does mean is higher prosperity. If you want high taxation, reduce; the duties. Put them down 10 per cent, and instead of a surplus of $13,500,000 the Finance Minister will be able to show a surplus of $20,000,000. Import more goods and you will collect more duties, but that is not what the people want. We want to make our goods in this country.
Does the hon. gentleman think that increased protection will increase the price of lead. He says that increased protection will not increase the prices.
Ask Mr. Galliher.
That is a pretty heavy question.
I think it is.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding) moved the adjournment of the House.
I would ask the government if they have received any report respecting the subject of the startling rumour which has been in circulation, of a volcanic eruption in the North-west Territories ?

I regret to say, Sir, that I am not in a position to add anything to the information given in the public press. The Prime Minister received a short telegram concerning the matter this afternoon, and instructions were at once given to inquire for further particulars. We hope that by to-morrow's sitting we may be in a position to give further information.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.55 p.m.
Thursday, April 30, 1903.
